Write the equations as on paper, simulate them, find where the flow becomes unstable, follow its orbits and bifurcations. heading: The equation on the page is the equation that runs
text: Conatus reads the problem as mathematics, compiles it for the CPU or the GPU, and tells you exactly what it did. Nothing changes behind your back. Below, the first tutorial as it ran, and what it printed. t01_orr_sommerfeld.py (excerpt) Copy line = cn . Box ( y = cn . walls ( - 1 , 1 ) ) # wall-normal coordinate y in [-1, 1] m = cn . Model ( line , name = "Orr-Sommerfeld" , Re = 1e4 , alpha = 1.0 ) m . scalar ( "v" ) # v(y) exp(i alpha (x - c t)), wall-normal velocity m . given ( U = lambda y : 1 - y * * 2 ) # plane Poiseuille base flow (depends on y) m . eigenvalue ( "c" , growth = "imag" ) # wave speed c: a mode grows with Im c m . define ( "L2(f) = dy(dy(f)) - alpha**2*f" ) # D^2 - alpha^2 m . equations ( "Orr_Sommerfeld: L2(L2(v))/(1j*alpha*Re) - U*L2(v) + dy(dy(U))*v + c*L2(v) = 0" ) m . at ( "walls" , "v = 0" , "dy(v) = 0" ) # rigid walls at y = -1 and y = 1 print ( m . explain ( full = True ) ) # every automatic decision (taus, modes) res = m . eigenvalues ( N = 64 , drift = 96 , drift_tol = 1e-6 ) # keep modes found again at N = 96 i = int ( res . values . imag . argmax ( ) ) # least stable surviving mode print ( res . explain ( key = "imag" ) ) print ( f "c = {res.values[i]:.10f} backward residual {res.residuals[i]:.1e}" ) Output c = 0.2375264888+0.0037396706j backward residual 4.2e-16 Re_c = 5772.2218 alpha_c = 1.020547 [PASS] right residual: 5.02e-20 (threshold 1e-12) — ||(L + sigma M) x|| backward error [PASS] spectral tail: 1.72e-10 (threshold 1e-08) — last 4 Chebyshev coefficients / max (mode resolved in N) OK: c and Re_c agree with Orszag (1971) to the published digits; alpha_c within 2e-5 Declare the domain, the fields and the equations, as written on paper. Discretise and check. A rank report refuses a missing or extra boundary condition before anything runs. Solve, and see how far to trust it. Every result comes with its own checks. What it does

heading: Getting started
text: Tutorial 0 Getting started with Conatus One problem from beginning to end: a layer of fluid heated from below. You will write its equations as on paper, ask whether the fluid at rest is stable, find where convection starts to the digits of the published value, then simulate the rolls that appear above onset and measure the heat they carry. About half an hour, on a laptop. On this page Install Write the model Read what Conatus decided Is the fluid at rest stable? Where convection starts Simulate above onset Steady rolls The Methods paragraph and the run On a GPU The checks What next Everything below is one Python script, shown piece by piece. It ran as shown, and each output is what it printed. The whole script is in the documentation ; run it with python t00_getting_started.py .

heading: 1 . Install
text: Conatus needs Linux x86-64 and Python 3.11, 3.12 or 3.13 (3.12 recommended); the wheel carries its compiled core, so no compiler is needed. The tutorials extra adds matplotlib, which draws this tutorial's figure. The last line checks the installation and says what this machine can run: the compiled core, a GPU. Copy Copy $ python3.12 -m venv venv && . venv/bin/activate $ pip install "conatus[tutorials]" # the CPU wheel, compiled core included (+ matplotlib for the figures) $ python -m conatus doctor # what this machine can run, and what is missing For a GPU, see Install : the CUDA 12 wheel (beta) of the same release.

heading: 2 . Write the model
text: Rayleigh–Bénard convection is the flow of a fluid layer between a hot plate below and a cold plate above. Warm fluid is lighter and wants to rise; viscosity and heat diffusion hold it back. In the Boussinesq approximation, with lengths in units of the layer depth and times in units of the thermal diffusion time, the velocity u , the pressure p and the temperature T obey ∂ t u + u ·∇ u = −∇ p + Pr ∇² u + Pr Ra T e z ∇· u = 0 ∂ t T + u ·∇ T = ∇² T u = 0 and T = ±½ on the plates z = ∓½ Two numbers set the physics: the Rayleigh number Ra, the strength of the heating against the two diffusions, and the Prandtl number Pr, the ratio of viscosity to heat diffusivity. In Conatus the model is these lines: Copy t00_getting_started.py Copy import numpy as np import conatus as cn from conatus . expert import critical def convection ( Ra ) : "" "Rayleigh-Benard convection between two plates; one roll pair fits the box of length 2." "" box = cn . Box ( x = cn . periodic ( 2.0 ) , z = cn . walls ( - 0.5 , 0.5 ) ) # x periodic, plates at z = -1/2, 1/2 m = cn . Model ( box , name = "Rayleigh-Benard" , Ra = Ra , Pr = 1 ) m . velocity ( "u" ) , m . pressure ( "p" ) , m . scalar ( "T" ) m . equations ( "" " momentum : dt ( u ) + grad ( p ) - Pr * lap ( u ) = Pr * Ra * T * ez - u · grad ( u ) continuity : div ( u ) = 0 heat : dt ( T ) - lap ( T ) = - u · grad ( T ) "" " ) m . at ( "bottom" , u = 0 , T = + 0.5 ) # hot plate below, no slip m . at ( "top" , u = 0 , T = - 0.5 ) # cold plate above, no slip return m m = convection ( Ra = 2500 ) print ( m . explain ( ) ) Read it as you would read the equations. cn.Box declares the domain: periodic in x with length 2 (one pair of counter-rotating rolls), between walls at z = ±½. The domain names its boundaries, bottom and top . The model declares its unknowns (a velocity, a pressure, a scalar) and its parameters, then the equations in a string, written as on paper: u·grad(u) is the advection, ez the vertical unit vector. The conditions are stated where they hold. There is no basis to choose, no resolution yet, and nothing to say about how the boundary conditions are imposed.

heading: 3 . Read what Conatus decided
text: Some decisions are needed to turn the model into a computation. Conatus makes them by fixed rules, and explain() lists every one. A few lines of its report: m.explain() (excerpt) Time stepping: 7 linear term(s) implicit; nonlinear terms explicit (momentum, heat) Boundary conditions: bottom: u = 0, T = 0.5; top: u = 0, T = -0.5 (tau method, placed automatically) Gauge: the mean of p is fixed (integ(p) = 0) Dealiasing: x: 3/2, z: 3/2 (declared default for products of degree 2) Linear terms are treated implicitly and nonlinear ones explicitly; m.explain(full=True) lists every term with the side it went to and why. Each boundary condition is attached to the equation where its unknown has its highest derivative across the walls. The pressure is recognised from the structure of the equations, not from its name, and its free constant is fixed. Dealiasing uses the standard 3/2 rule, said aloud. Anything the rules cannot decide is refused with a message that says what to write instead: nothing is guessed.

heading: 4 . Is the fluid at rest stable?
text: With the plates at fixed temperatures, the fluid can stay at rest while heat simply conducts through it: T = − z , u = 0. Whether it does depends on Ra. Ask the model for the normal modes of small disturbances to that state, for the rolls that fit the box (wavenumber k = π): Copy Copy growth = { } for Ra in ( 1500 , 2500 ) : lin = convection ( Ra ) . linearize ( about = { "u" : 0 , "T" : lambda z : - z } ) # fluid at rest, T = -z modes = lin . eigenvalues ( N = 24 , k = np . pi ) # 24 Chebyshev modes across, roll wavenumber pi growth [ Ra ] = modes . values . real . max ( ) print ( f "Ra = {Ra}: largest growth rate {growth[Ra]:+.6f}" ) Output Ra = 1500: largest growth rate -1.637012 Ra = 2500: largest growth rate +5.542506 linearize derives the linear equations from the ones you wrote; eigenvalues solves them with 24 Chebyshev modes across the layer. Here you choose the resolution: Conatus never does. At Ra = 1500 every disturbance decays; at Ra = 2500 one grows. Convection starts in between.

heading: 5 . Where convection starts
text: To find the threshold, write the problem as it appears in textbooks. A disturbance of wavenumber k behaves as e ikx + st ; its vertical velocity w ( z ) and temperature θ( z ) satisfy two ordinary differential equations in which s is the eigenvalue. This is a model on a line, with the eigenvalue declared: Copy Copy onset = cn . Model ( cn . Box ( z = cn . walls ( - 0.5 , 0.5 ) ) , name = "convection onset" , Ra = 1700.0 , k = 3.1 , Pr = 1 ) onset . scalar ( "w" ) , onset . scalar ( "theta" ) # w(z), theta(z) times exp(i k x + s t) onset . eigenvalue ( "s" , growth = "real" ) onset . define ( "L(f) = dz(dz(f)) - k**2*f" ) # the Laplacian of one Fourier mode onset . equations ( "" " momentum : s * L ( w ) = Pr * L ( L ( w ) ) - Pr * Ra * k * * 2 * theta heat : s * theta = w + L ( theta ) "" " ) onset . at ( "walls" , "w = 0" , "dz(w) = 0" , "theta = 0" ) # drift=48: a mode counts only if it is found again at 48 modes (spurious tau modes are not) P = onset . parametric ( N = 32 , over = ( "Ra" , "k" ) , drift = 48 , drift_tol = 1e-6 ) crit = critical ( P , "Ra" , bracket = ( 1500 , 2000 ) , over = { "k" : ( 2.8 , 3.4 ) } , xtol = 1e-9 ) print ( f "Ra_c = {crit.value:.4f} k_c = {crit.over['k']:.5f}" ) Output Ra_c = 1707.7618 k_c = 3.11632 parametric keeps Ra and k as live parameters of the discretised problem; critical finds the Ra at which the least stable mode stops decaying, and minimises it over k . The filter abs(s) < 100 is a declared choice: it sets aside the spurious modes that boundary conditions add to any polynomial discretisation, far out in the spectrum. The result is the classical onset of convection between rigid plates, Ra c = 1707.762 at k c = 3.117 (Reid & Harris 1958; Chandrasekhar 1961), to every published digit.

heading: 6 . Simulate above onset
text: Back to the full equations, at Ra = 2500. A simulation needs a resolution, a time-stepping scheme and a time step: three arguments, never defaults. Start from the conduction state with a tiny roll, and measure how fast it grows: Copy Copy sim = m . simulate ( N = ( 32 , 24 ) , scheme = "RK443" , dt = 5e-4 ) sim . initial ( T = lambda x , z : - z + 1e-6 * np . cos ( np . pi * x ) * np . cos ( np . pi * z ) ) def roll_amplitude ( sim ) : "" "Largest departure of T from its horizontal mean: the size of the rolls." "" T = sim . grid ( "T" ) return np . abs ( T - T . mean ( axis = 0 ) ) . max ( ) sim . run ( until = 0.3 ) a1 , t1 = roll_amplitude ( sim ) , sim . t sim . run ( until = 0.8 ) a2 , t2 = roll_amplitude ( sim ) , sim . t sigma = np . log ( a2 / a1 ) / ( t2 - t1 ) print ( f "measured growth rate {sigma:.6f} eigenvalue {growth[2500]:.6f}" ) Output measured growth rate 5.542508 eigenvalue 5.542506 The simulation and the eigenvalue problem are two different computations from the same model; while the disturbance is small they must agree, and they do, to the sixth digit. run(until=...) refuses a time that is not a whole number of steps rather than change the step behind your back.

heading: 7 . Steady rolls
text: Let the rolls grow until the nonlinear terms stop them. The run is recorded in a registry as it goes (next section). Then measure the Nusselt number Nu, the heat carried across the layer in units of what conduction alone would carry, three ways: averaged over the layer, and through each plate. Copy Copy from conatus . diagnostics import Chebyshev , Grid , Periodic grid = Grid ( [ Periodic ( 2.0 , 32 ) , Chebyshev ( - 0.5 , 0.5 , 24 ) ] ) # the simulation's grid points profile = Grid ( [ Chebyshev ( - 0.5 , 0.5 , 24 ) ] ) # functions of z alone def nusselt ( sim ) : "" "Heat carried across the layer in units of conduction, measured three ways." "" w , T = sim . grid ( "u" ) [ 1 ] , sim . grid ( "T" ) layer = 1 + float ( grid . mean ( w * T ) ) # conduction + convection, averaged over the layer dTdz = profile . cheb_coeffs ( profile . d ( T . mean ( axis = 0 ) , 0 ) , 0 ) bottom = - np . polynomial . chebyshev . chebval ( - 1.0 , dTdz ) # conduction through each plate top = - np . polynomial . chebyshev . chebval ( + 1.0 , dTdz ) return layer , bottom , top with cn . runs . track ( "rb_Ra2500" , tags = [ "getting-started" ] , root = "runs" ) as run : sim . solver . run ( round ( ( 6.0 - sim . t ) / sim . dt ) , record = run ) # on to t = 6 Nu_layer , Nu_bottom , Nu_top = nusselt ( sim ) run . result ( Nu = Nu_layer ) print ( f "t = {sim.t:.1f}: Nu = {Nu_layer:.6f} (layer) {Nu_bottom:.6f} (bottom plate) " f "{Nu_top:.6f} (top plate)" ) Output t = 6.0: Nu = 1.474455 (layer) 1.474455 (bottom plate) 1.474455 (top plate) In a steady state the heat that enters through the hot plate leaves through the cold one, and crosses every level in between: the three numbers agree. The rolls carry about half as much heat again as conduction. The saturated rolls at Ra = 2500: temperature departure from conduction (red warm, green cool) and isotherms. Drawn by the script from the computed field.

heading: 8 . The Methods paragraph and the run
text: Every simulation can describe itself: sim.methods() writes the paragraph of a paper that says how the result was computed, with its references. Its opening: The IVP 'Rayleigh-Benard' for (u, p, T) was solved with Conatus. The domain is discretized as follows: x ∈ [0, 2) is periodic and expanded in a real (cosine/sine) Fourier series of 32 modes; z ∈ [-0.5, 0.5] is expanded in 24 Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind. Derivatives, basis conversions and multiplications by non-constant coefficients use the sparse, banded ultraspherical operators of Olver & Townsend, and boundary conditions are imposed with the generalized tau method (4 tau variable(s), each entering through a lift polynomial), following Burns et al. … The with cn.runs.track(...) block above kept the run in a registry (a folder, here runs ): the problem, the numerics, the parameters, the code version, the start and end states, and the results you attach. Later, cn.runs.find(Nu__gt=1.4) finds it again, compare shows what differs between two runs, and reproduce checks a rerun bit for bit. See the run registry .

heading: 9 . On a GPU
text: The same model runs on an NVIDIA GPU with one more argument, backend="cuda" ; the results agree with the CPU to rounding. From the GPU tutorial, which compares the two: Copy t02b_rayleigh_benard_gpu.py (excerpt) Copy runs , early = { } , { } for label , kw in [ ( "cpu" , dict ( backend = "cpu" ) ) , ( "gpu" , dict ( backend = "cuda" , f_backend = "fused" ) ) ] : # both choices explicit s = m . simulate ( N = ( 128 , 64 ) , scheme = "RK443" , dt = 2e-4 , * * kw ) s . initial ( T = T_init ) s . run ( steps = 20 ) # compare here: rounding not yet amplified early [ label ] = s . grid ( "T" ) . copy ( ) t0 = time . perf_counter ( ) s . run ( steps = 180 ) # timing (the flow becomes strongly nonlinear) runs [ label ] = ( s , ( time . perf_counter ( ) - t0 ) / 180 ) print ( f "{label}: {1e3 * runs[label][1]:.2f} ms per step" ) print ( runs [ "gpu" ] [ 0 ] . explain ( ) ) Output (GPU) after 20 steps: relative max |T_cpu - T_gpu| = 8.6e-15; graph vs plain = 0.0e+00 To watch a run while it computes, from a browser or a phone, declare what to show with sim.watch(...) : see the user guide.

heading: 10 . The checks
text: The script ends by checking itself against the literature and against the identities above. If Conatus ever stopped reproducing them, the script would fail: the outputs on this page come from its last execution, which passed. Copy Copy RA_C , K_C = 1707.762 , 3.117 # Reid & Harris (1958); Chandrasekhar (1961) assert abs ( crit . value - RA_C ) < 1e-3 and abs ( crit . over [ "k" ] - K_C ) < 1e-3 , crit assert growth [ 1500 ] < 0 < growth [ 2500 ] , growth assert abs ( sigma - growth [ 2500 ] ) < 1e-5 , ( sigma , growth [ 2500 ] ) assert Nu_layer > 1 and abs ( Nu_bottom - Nu_layer ) < 1e-3 * Nu_layer \ and abs ( Nu_top - Nu_layer ) < 1e-3 * Nu_layer , ( Nu_layer , Nu_bottom , Nu_top ) print ( "OK: onset at Reid & Harris' Ra_c and k_c; the simulation grows at the eigenvalue's rate " "and saturates into rolls carrying the same heat through both plates" ) Output OK: onset at Reid & Harris' Ra_c and k_c; the simulation grows at the eigenvalue's rate and saturates into rolls carrying the same heat through both plates

heading: 11 . What next
text: Things to try with this script: raise Ra and measure how Nu grows (a faster flow may need a smaller time step: sim.cfl() suggests one, it never imposes one); change Pr; make the box longer, cn.periodic(4.0) , and see which roll pair grows first. Other domains, a disk or a spherical shell, are one line each: see Geometries and, for shells, the user guide . heading: Docs
text: Documentation Documentation The reference: each part of Conatus described once, with the choices you make and the ones it will not make for you. To learn, start with the Tutorials .

heading: Getting started
text: Tutorial 0: one problem from the equations to a published result, every step executed.

heading: Install
text: On CPU or with CUDA, and how to check what your machine can run.

heading: Tutorials
text: All the tutorials, each a script ending on a result from the literature. User guide

heading: Geometries
text: A geometry says where the problem lives: its coordinates, which directions are periodic, where the walls are and what they are called.

heading: Spherical shells
text: The space between two concentric spheres, where planets and stars convect: simulations on a CPU or a GPU, rotating convection, exact adjoints and optimal perturbations, with the same model text as in a box.

heading: Channels between two surfaces
text: A channel whose walls are not flat: a wavy bottom, a bump, a corrugated lid.

heading: Equations
text: A model is written as on paper: unknowns, parameters, known fields and equations in text, with terms on whichever side you like.

heading: Boundary conditions
text: Conditions are declared by boundary name, as on paper; Conatus decides how each one enters the discrete system and prints that decision.

heading: Ready problems
text: cn.problems gives the canonical flows and model equations ready to solve, each validated against a published value.

heading: Units and conventions
text: Unit systems make every change of nondimensionalisation an explicit, checked call. User guide

heading: Simulations and time steppers
text: A model with dt(...) is integrated by m.simulate(...), with the resolution, the scheme and the time step written in the call.

heading: Resolution
text: The resolution report says, for each unknown and each direction, whether the spectral coefficients have decayed, and how many modes a target accuracy would need.

heading: GPU
text: The same model runs on an NVIDIA GPU by adding backend="cuda"; the arithmetic is double precision, as on the CPU.

heading: Diagnostics and visualization
text: Eulerian, Lagrangian and mixing diagnostics computed from the fields of a run, on the CPU or the GPU.

heading: Particles and dye of a simulation
text: Tracer particles and a numerical dye that live inside a native simulation: they advance with each step of sim.run, on the CPU or the GPU, and write files in the cn.io layout.

heading: Input and output
text: Two kinds of HDF5 files: analysis files, which hold what you asked to see (fields, derived quantities, numbers) at a fixed cadence, and checkpoints, which hold everything needed to continue a run exactly.

heading: Notebooks
text: In Jupyter, Conatus objects display as formatted tables and cards. User guide

heading: Eigenvalues and stability
text: Normal modes of a linear problem, each with its backward residual, with spurious modes removed only by a declared test.

heading: Onset of convection
text: The critical Rayleigh number of Rayleigh–Bénard convection between no-slip walls, and the shape of its mode, in a few calls: from the ready linearization, then from the equations of a normal mode written by hand.

heading: Non-modal analysis
text: Transient growth of a linear operator, measured in the kinetic-energy norm.

heading: Invariant solutions
text: Equilibria, travelling waves and periodic orbits found by Newton–Krylov–hookstep on the flow map of your own time stepper.

heading: Continuation and bifurcations
text: Branches of solutions followed through folds by pseudo-arclength, with branch points, Hopf points, cycles and codimension-two curves located on the way.

heading: Floquet analysis
text: Stability of time-periodic flows by the Hill method: the Floquet exponents are eigenvalues of one large, structured problem.

heading: Chaos and ensembles
text: Lyapunov exponents with error bars, covariant Lyapunov vectors, Poincaré maps, and the fate of many trajectories integrated as one batch.

heading: Invariant manifolds and slices
text: The unstable manifold of an equilibrium as a polynomial parametrization, connections between solutions, and the reduction of a continuous symmetry by a slice.

heading: Symmetry subspaces
text: Computing in an invariant subspace of a symmetry group: fewer unknowns and isolated solutions, at the price of hiding what breaks the symmetry.

heading: Adjoints and sensitivity
text: Exact tangent and adjoint of the discrete time stepper, adjoint eigenmodes in a declared inner product, the wavemaker and the sensitivity to the base flow.

heading: Tangent, adjoint and optimal perturbations
text: FlowMap is the time-stepping map of a solver, X_0 ↦ X_N, with its exact discrete tangent (jvp) and adjoint (vjp): the same schemes, the same operators, the same linear factorizations, transposed.

heading: Data-driven analysis
text: Dynamic mode decomposition and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition of snapshots, in the inner product of the physics rather than that of the array. User guide

heading: explain() and the Methods paragraph
text: Every key object says, in plain text, what it is and which numerical choices it carries, and a simulation writes the Methods paragraph of your paper from what it actually ran.

heading: Numerical uncertainty
text: A number computed by a simulation (a growth rate, a mean, a value at a point) depends on the resolution and on the time step.

heading: The run registry
text: cn.runs records the computations you may want to find, compare, cite or re-run later, with their numerics, code and machine.

heading: Reproducibility and provenance
text: A number is only useful if you can say which code, which numerics and which machine produced it; Conatus records this when the computation runs, not afterwards.

heading: Checking an installation
text: python -m conatus doctor says what your machine can run (compiled core, GPU) and, for anything missing, what to do.

heading: Errors and what they mean
text: Every error says what is wrong, where, why it is refused, and what to write instead. User guide

heading: Coming from Dedalus
text: If you know Dedalus, you already know how to write a Conatus model; what changes is what you no longer write, and what you can do with the model afterwards. User guide

heading: The expert layer
text: Under every native model there is an explicit problem that you can read, modify or write yourself: bases with their sizes, tau terms, the left and right sides of each equation.

heading: IR and operators
text: The expert layer writes problems with Python objects: fields, parameters and operators that build an exact symbolic expression.

heading: Bases and domains
text: In the expert layer a domain is a coordinate system with one spectral basis per coordinate, each with its size and dealiasing factor.

heading: Tau terms by hand
text: In the expert layer you place the boundary terms yourself; a rank check refuses an ill-posed system before any factorisation.

heading: API reference
text: Every public object, from its docstring: the user layer, then the expert layer.

heading: Mathematics
text: The methods behind Conatus: discretisation, time stepping, eigenproblems, orbits, continuation. Next Capabilities → Everything Conatus does, in one page.

heading: Install
text: Install Install Conatus 0.1.0 installs with pip from a binary wheel, with its compiled core inside: no compiler needed. The CPU wheel is on PyPI; a CUDA 12 wheel for NVIDIA GPUs, in beta, is attached to the GitHub release . It also builds from source.

heading: Requirements
text: System Linux x86-64. Python 3.11, 3.12 or 3.13: 3.12 runs the whole test suite; on all three the wheel installs, imports, solves a problem and passes doctor in a clean manylinux_2_28 image; 3.12 is recommended. A newer Python is refused until it is tested. Python dependencies NumPy ≥ 1.26, SciPy ≥ 1.11, SymPy ≥ 1.12, h5py ≥ 3.8, installed by pip; matplotlib ≥ 3.7 with the tutorials extra. Wheels Linux x86-64 with glibc 2.28 or newer (RHEL 8, Ubuntu 20.04 and later). The CUDA wheel needs an NVIDIA driver for CUDA 12.9 (≥ 575, or an older 12.x driver through minor-version compatibility); it pulls the CUDA runtime, cuFFT and cuBLAS as pip wheels (about 700 MB). Built for A100 (sm_80) and L40S (sm_89); beta. Build tools (from source) A C++20 compiler (GCC 13 from conda-forge), CMake ≥ 3.24, scikit-build-core and nanobind (fetched by pip). LAPACK, BLAS From conda-forge, in the active environment; the build looks nowhere else, so you always know which libraries you use. The core has no FFT library of its own: CPU transforms are NumPy/SciPy, GPU transforms cuFFT. GPU (optional) An NVIDIA GPU; to build from source, the CUDA 12 toolkit (nvcc, cuFFT, cuBLAS) from conda-forge.

heading: CPU
text: Copy $ python3.12 -m venv venv && . venv/bin/activate $ pip install "conatus[tutorials]" # CPU wheel from PyPI + matplotlib for the tutorials $ python -m conatus doctor # what this machine can run

heading: GPU (CUDA 12, beta)
text: Copy # download the conatus-0.1.0+cu12-cp3XX-…whl of your Python from the GitHub release, then $ python3.12 -m venv venv && . venv/bin/activate $ pip install "./conatus-0.1.0+cu12-cp312-cp312-<platform>.whl[gpu,tutorials]" $ python -m conatus doctor # on a GPU node: "GPU (backend='cuda')": ok

heading: Create a conda environment with the compiled dependencies
text: Copy # LAPACK and BLAS come from the active conda env only (no system fallback) $ micromamba create -n conatus -c conda-forge python=3.12 gxx_linux-64=13 liblapack libblas $ micromamba activate conatus

heading: Build and install
text: pip install ".[tutorials]" compiles the C++20 core ( conatus._core , via scikit-build-core, CMake and nanobind), installs it inside the package with its dependencies (h5py included: outputs and checkpoints) and adds matplotlib, which the tutorials use for their figures. pip install . alone skips matplotlib. Copy $ git clone https://github.com/rubendahan/conatus && cd conatus $ pip install ".[tutorials]" # CPU (the default) + matplotlib for the tutorials

heading: Check
text: See Check your installation below.

heading: Start from the CPU environment and add the CUDA toolkit
text: Copy # in the same env: nvcc, cuFFT, cuBLAS and CuPy from conda-forge (CUDA 12.9 tested) $ micromamba install -c conda-forge cuda-version=12.9 cuda-nvcc cuda-cudart-dev libcufft-dev libcublas-dev cupy-core

heading: Build with the CUDA backend
text: The CUDA backend is switched on at build time. CuPy comes from conda here: do not add the gpu extra, which would install a second CuPy from pip. Copy $ pip install . -Ccmake.define.CONATUS_CUDA=ON \ -Ccmake.define.CMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER=$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/nvcc \ -Ccmake.define.CMAKE_CUDA_HOST_COMPILER=$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/x86_64-conda-linux-gnu-g++ \ -Ccmake.define.CUDAToolkit_ROOT=$CONDA_PREFIX # to target your GPU architecture, add # -Ccmake.define.CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=<your arch>

heading: Check on a GPU node
text: If the GPU cannot be used, Conatus says why: the core was built without CUDA, or no device is visible.

heading: Optional extras
text: Extras add optional Python packages; they are combined as usual, e.g. pip install "conatus[tutorials,notebook]" . Extra Adds For tutorials matplotlib ≥ 3.7 The figures of the tutorials (the optional Dedalus check of tutorial 14 needs Dedalus). gpu cupy-cuda12x ≥ 13 Device arrays, with the CUDA wheel (a source build also needs CONATUS_CUDA=ON). notebook ipywidgets ≥ 8 Rich displays of explain() in Jupyter. dedalus-compare dedalus ≥ 3.0 Side-by-side comparisons with Dedalus. docs sphinx ≥ 7, myst-parser ≥ 2 Building the documentation site. dev pytest ≥ 8, ruff ≥ 0.5, mpmath ≥ 1.3 Tests and lint. all tutorials, notebook, gpu, docs, dev Everything above except dedalus-compare.

heading: Check your installation
text: Copy $ python -m conatus doctor # what this machine can run (compiled core, GPU), and what to do about what is missing $ python -c "import conatus.expert as ex; print(ex.explain())" # what the single import contains, and any name clash $ python -c "import conatus.runtime as r; print(r.CORE_SOURCE)" installed # CUDA wheel or build only: True on a node with a visible GPU $ python -c "from conatus.runtime import cuda; print(cuda.available())" doctor tells you what this machine can run and how to fix what is missing. Conatus always says which compiled core it loaded; it never switches to another copy behind your back. An installed package writes nothing inside its environment: live-monitoring data go to ~/.cache/conatus (or $XDG_CACHE_HOME , CN_CACHE , CN_TMP ), and doctor prints these directories. Then start the tutorials with tutorial 0, getting started. Next Tutorial 0: getting started → Your first model, from the equations to the onset of convection.

heading: Capabilities
text: Capabilities What you can do with Conatus Write the equations, run them where you like, and let Conatus find the structure of the solutions: instabilities, orbits, bifurcations. Everything below is available from the same language of equations. Write Discretise Run Analyse Keep track Write

heading: The language of equations
text: You write the problem the way it is written on paper. Conatus understands it as mathematics and explains what it built.

heading: Equations as on paper
text: Domains, fields, parameters and equations in their usual form; boundary conditions by the name of the boundary. What Conatus places for you, it lists.

heading: Refused, not repaired
text: A missing or extra boundary condition, an ill-posed split or an undeclared choice is refused with a message that says what, where and why, and proposes a fix it never applies itself.

heading: Exact derivatives, for free
text: Every expression knows its derivative and its adjoint, so linearisations, tangents and adjoints follow from the equations you wrote. Discretise

heading: Spectral accuracy, in any geometry
text: Sparse spectral methods, from the channel to the ball, with bases that are regular by construction.

heading: Boxes, channels and infinite lines
text: Fourier and Chebyshev directions; sine and cosine series for stress-free or fixed-temperature walls, with no boundary terms at all; Hermite and Laguerre functions on the whole and the half line; compound intervals for interior layers; mapped bases and complex paths for inviscid modes. Geometries →

heading: Disks, pipes, spheres, shells and balls
text: Curved geometries without axis conditions or fixes at the poles: every field is regular by construction. Rigid or stress-free walls are one declaration. Geometries →

heading: Symmetries that halve the work
text: Declare a reflection or a rotation and Conatus solves in the symmetric subspace, after checking that the equations respect it. Run

heading: On a laptop or a GPU
text: The same model runs on a CPU or a GPU. Resolution, scheme and time step are yours to choose, never guessed.

heading: Time integration
text: Implicit–explicit schemes, multistep (backward differentiation and Crank–Nicolson) and Runge–Kutta: the schemes of Dedalus, with the same numbers. Boundary values that move in time are imposed at every stage: second order or better for every scheme (RK443 about 2.8), where the usual convention falls to first order. Exact restarts from a checkpoint. Tutorial 0, step 6 →

heading: GPU-native
text: One keyword moves a simulation to the GPU, in a box, a channel, a disk, a pipe, on a sphere, in a ball or a spherical shell; nonlinear terms become fused kernels, and in boxes, channels and shells whole steps can be replayed as one graph. Analyse

heading: The dynamical system behind the equations
text: The problem you simulate is also a dynamical system: Conatus finds its structure.

heading: Stability
text: Eigenvalues with their residuals, critical parameters and sensitivities, with spurious modes removed in the open. Dynamics →

heading: Orbits and bifurcations
text: Equilibria, travelling waves and periodic orbits; branches followed through folds, pitchforks and Hopf points. Dynamics →

heading: Time-periodic flows
text: Floquet exponents and optimal transient growth about any flow that repeats in time, written as a function of time, such as pulsatile flow in a channel. Dynamics →

heading: Adjoints and transient growth
text: Exact adjoints of the time stepper, in boxes, channels and the spherical shell, for gradients and optimisation; linear and nonlinear optimal perturbations of non-normal flows. Dynamics → Keep track

heading: Observable and reproducible
text: A computation you can find again afterwards.

heading: Every run recorded
text: Parameters, code version and results are kept for each run; find, compare and reproduce them later.

heading: Files any tool can read
text: Snapshots and checkpoints in HDF5, with the provenance of the run inside; a run split over several jobs continues exactly as if it had never stopped. Input and output →

heading: A number with its error bar
text: From the resolutions and time steps you declare, a computed quantity is reported with an error estimate and the checks behind it; time averages come with their statistical error. Numerical uncertainty →

heading: A Methods paragraph, written for you
text: Each computation can describe itself: the discretisation, the scheme and the references, ready for a paper. How these capabilities compare with published results and independent codes is on the validation page . Next Dynamics → Stability, bifurcations, periodic orbits and Floquet analysis.

heading: Dynamics
text: Dynamics The dynamical system behind the equations The equations you write for a simulation also define a dynamical system. Conatus lets you ask it the questions that matter: where it becomes unstable, how its solutions branch, which orbits organise it, how it answers a push. Same equations, no problem-specific code. Where a flow becomes unstable Symmetry subspaces Bifurcations, followed Equilibria, travelling waves and periodic orbits Time-periodic flows: Floquet analysis Transient growth Chaos: Lyapunov exponents and ensembles Adjoints, sensitivity and data

heading: Where a flow becomes unstable
text: Linearise the equations you already wrote about a base state and ask for their eigenmodes, with left eigenvectors and the residual of each. Follow the least stable one as a parameter changes and find the critical point where it starts to grow. Modes that do not survive a finer resolution are removed, and you are told. Tutorial 1 : A first eigenvalue problem: Orr–Sommerfeld · Tutorial 8 : Polar geometry: a drum, a pipe, two rotating cylinders

heading: Symmetry subspaces
text: Declare a reflection or a rotation and solve in the symmetric subspace: the same eigenvalues for a fraction of the cost, after a check that the equations respect the symmetry. Tutorial 3 : Symmetries and symmetry subspaces

heading: Bifurcations, followed
text: Follow a branch of steady solutions as a parameter moves, through folds, by pseudo-arclength continuation. Pitchforks and Hopf points are detected and located on the way; switch branches, follow the cycles born at a Hopf point, continue a fold or a Hopf point in two parameters, and read the normal form that says what happens next. Tutorial 4 : Nonlinear boundary-value problems and continuation: Bratu · Tutorial 10 : Bifurcations: branch switching, cycles, codimension 2, normal forms

heading: Equilibria, travelling waves and periodic orbits
text: Find the invariant solutions that organise a turbulent or chaotic flow, from a guess or from the state of a running simulation, by Newton–Krylov with a hookstep, and compute their stability. Each solution is reported with its residual. Tutorial 5 : Invariant solutions: Kuramoto–Sivashinsky, L = 22

heading: Time-periodic flows: Floquet analysis
text: When the base flow oscillates, as in a pulsating channel or pipe, stability is a question about periodic motion. Conatus answers it with a Floquet–Hill method (Fourier in time, spectral in space), for any time-periodic linear problem written in the same language: give the base flow as a function of time and its period, and ask for its Floquet exponents or its optimal growth.

heading: Transient growth
text: Stable flows can still amplify a disturbance enormously before it decays. Find the optimal perturbation and its growth, about a steady or a time-periodic base flow, in the energy norm you declare.

heading: Chaos: Lyapunov exponents and ensembles
text: Lyapunov spectra, covariant vectors, the Kaplan–Yorke dimension, Poincaré maps and basins of attraction, from ensembles of trajectories integrated together. Tutorial 12 : Chaos and ensembles: Lyapunov spectrum, covariant vectors, Poincaré map, basins

heading: Adjoints, sensitivity and data
text: The physical adjoint of an operator in the inner product you declare (never a bare transpose), direct and adjoint global modes, the wavemaker and base-flow sensitivity; the exact adjoint of the time stepper for gradients, in a channel or a spherical shell, with the nonlinear optimal perturbation that grows most at a given energy. DMD and SPOD of data in the same norm. Tutorial 13 : Where a global mode is born, and what the data say about it The user guide describes each method in detail → All tutorials → Next Gallery → Flows computed with Conatus.

heading: Geometries
text: Geometries From the channel to the ball Every geometry speaks the same language: you name the domain, write the same equations, and name the boundaries where conditions hold. Conatus chooses the bases that belong to the geometry, regular at the axis and at the centre, and prints them with explain() .

heading: Declaring a domain
text: A geometry is one line. The rest of the model does not depend on it: the same equation in a box or in a ball differs only by this line and by the boundary names. a model on a disk Copy import conatus as cn disk = cn . Disk ( 1.0 ) # coordinates (phi, r), boundary "wall" m = cn . Model ( disk , name = "heat in a disk" , kappa = 1.0 ) T = m . scalar ( "T" ) m . equations ( "dt(T) - kappa*lap(T) = 0" ) m . at ( "wall" , T = 0 ) print ( m . explain ( ) ) # bases, conditions and their placement

heading: Box
text: cn.Box(x=cn.periodic(2.0), z=cn.walls(-0.5, 0.5)) Periodic directions and at most one direction between two walls. Fourier along periodic axes, Chebyshev between walls, or sine and cosine series (basis="sincos") when the walls are stress-free or held at a fixed value. Coordinates x, z (one to three axes, in the order written) Boundaries bottom, top, walls (or z=-0.5, z=0.5) Convection, Couette flow, boundary layers, pattern formation.

heading: Lines, half lines and compound intervals
text: cn.Box(x=cn.periodic(2.0), y=cn.half_line(scale=0.5)) Unbounded directions with the decay built into the basis (Hermite functions on the line, Laguerre functions on the half line); a width you choose, like a resolution. An interval cut into pieces, cn.walls(-1, -0.15, 0.15, 1), puts modes where a thin layer needs them, with continuity across the cuts added for you. Coordinates as named in the box Boundaries wall (the half line); none on cn.line(scale=...) Boundary layers over a plate, localised waves, fronts and interior layers.

heading: Channel
text: cn.Channel(2 * math.pi, math.pi) A box with walls at y = ±1, periodic in x and, in 3D, in z. Coordinates x, y, z (2D without the second length) Boundaries bottom, top, walls Plane Poiseuille and Couette flow, turbulent channels.

heading: Disk
text: cn.Disk(1.0) Regular at the centre by construction: no axis condition to add, nothing singular to guard against. Coordinates phi, r Boundaries wall Vortices, rotating tanks, flows in a circular cross-section.

heading: Annulus
text: cn.Annulus(1.0, 2.0) The gap between two circles. Coordinates phi, r Boundaries inner, outer, walls Taylor–Couette flow in a cross-section, rotating shear flows.

heading: Sphere
text: cn.Sphere(1.0) The surface of a sphere, regular at both poles. Coordinates phi, theta Boundaries none Shallow water, planetary waves, atmospheres.

heading: Spherical shell
text: cn.Shell(0.35, 1.0) The space between two spheres, where planets and stars convect. Simulations on a CPU or a GPU, exact adjoints and optimal perturbations, and rotating convection ready to run; the wall conditions are written in a form that stays stable at any radial resolution, and checked before the first step. Coordinates phi, theta, r Boundaries inner, outer, walls Rotating convection, dynamos, mantle and core flows, rotating shells. Spherical shells in the user guide →

heading: Ball
text: cn.Ball(1.0) The full sphere, regular at the centre by construction. Coordinates phi, theta, r Boundaries wall Flows in a spherical container, stellar interiors. Every wall takes rigid or stress-free conditions ( u=cn.free_slip ), curved walls included. Mapped bases, other polynomial families and hand-chosen bases are available in the expert layer; see the user guide . The gap between two rotating cylinders is cn.TaylorCouette(ri, ro, length) ; pipe flow and Taylor–Couette flow are also ready problems ( cn.problems ), as native models in cn.problems.native . To see the geometries at work, open the gallery . Next Gallery → The disk, the pipe, the shell and the sphere, computed.

heading: Dynamics
text: Periodic orbits, bifurcations, Floquet exponents and exact adjoints, including the spherical shell. Dynamics : test, value obtained, reference and deviation. heading: How these numbers are produced
text: Values are taken from the validation record of the release at every build of this site, never typed by hand. A dash in the deviation column means the row states the agreement in words rather than as one number.

heading: Coming next
text: Roadmap Coming next What is being built beyond 0.1.0. None of it is part of this release, and nothing here is a promise of a date or of a performance figure; each part will ship when it is validated like the rest of the library. For what 0.1.0 does today, see Capabilities .

heading: Multi-GPU runs across nodes
text: A distributed spectral solver that splits one simulation over several GPUs and several nodes, with the same model and the same script as on one GPU. It works and is being optimised; the exchange between nodes is where the work is.

heading: Conatus Studio
text: Watch and steer a running simulation from a browser, on a laptop or a phone: pause it, change a parameter, fork the run into a new branch, or seed a Newton search from the live state, without changing a bit of the computation it does not touch. A hosted hub with authenticated access connects the browser to runs on a cluster, without opening the cluster to the outside.

heading: An interface for AI agents
text: A compact, machine-readable description of the API and a JSON command-line entry point, so that an assistant can set up a run, check a script before it runs, and explain what a model, a solver or a result contains, from the same facts the library prints for a person.

heading: Further stability tools
text: Resolvent analysis and pseudospectra in a declared energy norm; periodic orbits of three-dimensional channel and pipe flows; certified counting of all eigenvalues inside a region of the complex plane by contour methods, so that no mode is missed; and high-resolution spherical shells.

heading: Citing
text: Citing How to cite Conatus If Conatus contributes to your work, please cite the software.

heading: Software
text: Copy BibTeX Copy @software{dahan2026conatus, author = {Dahan, Ruben}, title = {{Conatus: spectral PDEs and dynamical systems}}, year = {2026}, version = {0.1.0}, license = {BSD-3-Clause}, url = {https://github.com/rubendahan/conatus}, }

heading: Cite what you used
text: Every simulation can write the “Methods” paragraph of your paper from the objects themselves (resolution, boundary treatment, time stepper, tolerances), with its BibTeX, so the methods you used are cited as they were run. Conatus follows Dedalus (Burns et al. 2020) for its symbolic language and spectral methods; please cite it too when you rely on that design. Next Validation → Every published value Conatus reproduces.

Laguerre ( coord , size , start = 0.0 , scale = 1.0 , dealias = REQUIRED ) [source] ¶ Bases: Basis Laguerre functions on the half line x >= start: f(x) = sum_n c_n L_n(y) exp(-y/2), y = (x - start)/scale (orthonormal). heading: conatus.expert.PROTOCOL_VERSION
text: conatus.expert. PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1 ¶ int([x]) -> integer int(x, base=10) -> integer Convert a number or string to an integer, or return 0 if no arguments are given. If x is a number, return x.__int__(). For floating-point numbers, this truncates towards zero. If x is not a number or if base is given, then x must be a string, bytes, or bytearray instance representing an integer literal in the given base. The literal can be preceded by ‘+’ or ‘-’ and be surrounded by whitespace. The base defaults to 10. Valid bases are 0 and 2-36. Base 0 means to interpret the base from the string as an integer literal. >>> int(‘0b100’, base=0) 4

text: class conatus.expert. PolarCoordinates ( azimuth , radius ) [source] ¶ Bases: CoordinateSystem (phi, r) on the disk or annulus. Metric dr^2 + r^2 dphi^2. heading: conatus.expert.gain

heading: Expert layer: conatus.expert
text: import conatus.expert as ex # or: from conatus.expert import * The expert layer is the mathematical intermediate representation that native models compile to, together with every toolkit that operates on it. Use it to write a problem term by term (bases, tau variables and lifts chosen by hand), to reach options the native layer does not expose, or to apply a toolkit to m.compile(N).problem or sim.solver . A name reachable in both layers means the same thing in both: the same object, or, for discretize , linearize , methods and verify , the package cn.<name> whose call is the function conatus.expert.<name> ( cn.discretize(problem) works; cn.discretize.Plan too). conatus.api is the former name

heading: Citing Conatus

It is updated with the code; the version in the repository is the reference. R. heading: Cite the methods too
text: Conatus implements published methods; please cite them along with Conatus. You do not need to assemble the list by hand: plan.methods() writes a Methods paragraph for your run and returns the BibTeX entries of exactly the methods it used (for example Olver & Townsend 2013 for the ultraspherical operators, Burns et al. 2020 for the generalised tau method, Vasil et al. 2016 and 2019 for polar and spherical bases, Ascher, Ruuth & Spiteri 1997 for the IMEX Runge–Kutta schemes). See explain() and the Methods paragraph .

heading: Validation references
text: The published values reproduced by the tutorials and the gallery are listed on each page with their source. When you use Conatus to reproduce or extend one of them, cite the original work.

heading: Bases and domains
text: In the expert layer a domain is a coordinate system with one spectral basis per coordinate, each with its size and dealiasing factor. A Domain is a coordinate system and one basis per coordinate. Fourier directions are separable: the discrete problem splits into independent groups (one per wavenumber, or per azimuthal number \(m\) in polar geometry), each solved with banded Olver–Townsend operators.

heading: Dealiasing is always explicit
text: Every basis takes a dealias factor, and there is no default : from conatus.expert import CartesianCoordinates , Chebyshev z = CartesianCoordinates ( "z" )[ "z" ] try : Chebyshev ( z , 32 , ( - 1 , 1 )) except ValueError as err : print ( err ) # Chebyshev: dealias must be given explicitly # why: the dealiasing factor sets the grid of the nonlinear products; Conatus never picks it for you # fix: dealias=1 (no padding, linear problems) or dealias=3/2 (quadratic nonlinearities) try : Chebyshev ( z , 32 , ( - 1 , 1 ), dealias = True ) except TypeError as err : print ( err ) # Chebyshev: dealias=True/False is ambiguous; give the factor (1, 3/2, 2, ...) Linear problems (EVP, LBVP) use dealias=1 ; q

heading: Symmetry subspaces
text: A SymmetrySubspace(Reflection(z), T=EVEN, ...) passed to a problem ( symmetry= ) restricts every field to a declared parity, and each system shrinks to the size of the subspace. Parities are checked on every equation; an inconsistent declaration is refused. See 3. Symmetries and symmetry subspaces and Dynamics .

heading: Sine/cosine walls (native layer)

It is exact for stress-free walls, fixed-temperature or insulating walls, hinged plates: every unknown is a pure sine or cosine series, so its wall conditions hold identically and no tau term is needed. heading: How many conditions
text: Each unknown needs as many conditions as its order along the bounded coordinate, times the number of walls divided by two. A temperature with \(\nabla^2 T\) between two plates needs two; the Orr–Sommerfeld equation, fourth order in \(y\) , needs four (two per wall); in a disk, a ball or a pipe the centre is not a boundary, so a second-order unknown needs one condition at wall . A pressure that only appears under grad(p) needs none: Conatus recognises the incompressibility structure (below). A missing condition is refused before anything is built: import conatus as cn m = cn . Model ( cn . Box ( x = cn . walls ( 0 , 1 )), name = "heat" , kappa = 1.0 ) T = m . scalar ( "T" ) m . equations ( "d

heading: What Conatus does with them
text: Conatus imposes conditions with the tau method: each condition adds one unknown constant along the wall, which enters one equation through a fixed polynomial. You never write these terms. They are placed by one deterministic rule: each condition constrains one unknown; it goes into the equation where that unknown has its highest order along the bounded coordinate; inside that equation, the conditions fill the highest modes in the order you declared them. m.explain() lists every placement: Boundary conditions -> tau terms (automatic, deterministic): T = 0 at walls (left: x=0): tau_T1 lifted into mode N_x-1 of [0] eq0 -- T has its highest x-order (2) there T = 0 at walls (right: x=1): tau_T2 l

heading: When the rule cannot decide
text: Conatus refuses rather than guesses. Each message names the condition and the way out: Situation What to write the unknown has its highest order in two equations m.at(..., into="momentum") : name the equation that receives the condition a condition involves two unknowns, or none split it, or write the problem in the expert layer too many conditions for an unknown remove one (the extra one would perturb an equation) a scalar condition on one component of a vector unknown the expert layer ; a stress-free wall is u=cn.free_slip (below) an unknown boundary name one of the names listed by geometry.boundaries() Writing lift(...) yourself in a native model is refused: the placement is Conatus’s job

heading: Spurious modes in eigenvalue problems
text: Truncation creates a few spurious eigenvalues (very large, sometimes unstable). Conatus does not filter them with a hidden threshold. m.eigenvalues(N=64, drift=96, drift_tol=1e-6) solves the problem again at 96 modes and keeps only the eigenvalues found at both resolutions within the drift tolerance (yours, required: it decides which modes are returned); the result says how many were removed. A physical filter is allowed, but it is yours and it is logged: res.select(np.flatnonzero(abs(res.values) < 2), why="|c| < 2") . Worked example: 1. A first eigenvalue problem: Orr–Sommerfeld .

heading: Free-slip walls in the native layer
text: In the native layer ( cn.Model ) conditions are written by boundary name and the taus are placed for you. A stress-free wall is one declaration on the velocity: import conatus as cn box = cn . Box ( x = cn . periodic ( 2.0 ), z = cn . walls ( 0 , 1 )) free = cn . Model ( box , name = "RB stress-free" , Ra = 700 , Pr = 1 ) u , T = free . velocity ( "u" ), free . scalar ( "T" ) free . at ( "walls" , u = cn . free_slip , T = 0 ) # u·n = 0 and dz(u_t) = 0 at both walls rigid = cn . Model ( box , name = "RB rigid" , Ra = 2000 , Pr = 1 ) u , T = rigid . velocity ( "u" ), rigid . scalar ( "T" ) rigid . at ( "walls" , u = cn . no_slip , T = 0 ) # the same as u=0, named for symmetry slip = cn . Model

heading: Interfaces, half lines and the whole line
text: On a compound interval ( cn.walls(a, c, b) ) you declare the wall conditions only. For each unknown of order \(q\) the native layer adds, at every interface, the continuity of the value and of the derivatives up to \(q-1\) , written with one-sided traces, and gives each piece \(q\) tau terms in its last modes; explain() lists them (see Bases and domains ). In the IR the same conditions read import numpy as np from conatus.expert import ( LBVP , CartesianCoordinates , CompoundChebyshev , Domain , Field , diff , discretize , interp , lap , lift ) cs = CartesianCoordinates ( "x" ); x = cs [ "x" ] b = CompoundChebyshev ( x , ( 24 , 24 ), ( - 1 , 0.0 , 1 ), dealias = 1 ) # two pieces, interface x

heading: What you stop writing
text: Tau fields and lifts. Each condition is placed by a fixed rule, printed by explain() ( Boundary conditions ); the pressure gauge is recognised from the structure. Bases with sizes. The geometry fixes the bases; the number of modes is given when you solve. The split into left and right sides. Linear terms are implicit, nonlinear terms explicit, wherever you wrote them ( Equations ). The time loop. sim.run(until=t) with a fixed dt ; Conatus never adapts dt for you. What stays the same: the spectral method itself (Fourier, Chebyshev and curvilinear bases with sparse ultraspherical operators, the generalised tau method, IMEX schemes with Dedalus’s coefficients), the string syntax of the equation

heading: Importing a Dedalus script
text: cn.from_dedalus(script) translates a Dedalus 3 script into Conatus. You get back: the Conatus problem; the declared time stepping; the initial and given data; a line-by-line report . from pathlib import Path import conatus as cn Path ( "kdv_dedalus.py" ) . write_text ( """ import numpy as np import dedalus.public as d3 period, Nx, damping, dispersion = 8, 64, 3e-4, 5e-4 s = d3.Coordinate('x') mesh = d3.Distributor(s, dtype=np.float64) ring = d3.RealFourier(s, size=Nx, bounds=(0, period), dealias=1.5) h = mesh.Field(name='h', bases=ring) D = lambda F: d3.Differentiate(F, s) wave = d3.IVP([h], namespace=locals()) wave.add_equation("dt(h) - damping*D(D(h)) - dispersion*D(D(D(h))) = -h*D(h)") xs

heading: What happens to your script
text: The script is read, not run . Python’s ast module parses it, and a restricted interpreter walks it statement by statement. It understands: literals, arithmetic, tuples and lambdas; the dedalus.public names it knows; a whitelist of NumPy/SciPy functions, used for constants and initial data; the equation strings, which go through the Equations parser. No statement of the script is executed by Python, and Dedalus is never imported. Each statement gets one of four statuses: Status Meaning translated same mathematics and same method; the note lists any declared rewrite ( trace(grad(u)) -> div(u) ) or Dedalus default made explicit ( dealias=1 ) approximated translated, but the method differs in a

heading: The translated subset
text: Dedalus Conatus Note Coordinate , CartesianCoordinates , PolarCoordinates , Distributor(dtype=...) coordinate systems; field dtype process mesh and comm are ignored (parallel layout is decided at run time) RealFourier , ChebyshevT / Chebyshev , Legendre , Jacobi(a, b) same bases dealias omitted means Dedalus’s default of 1, written explicitly ComplexFourier(N) ComplexFourier(N) approximated : Dedalus keeps the Nyquist mode \(k=-N/2\) , Conatus drops it; that group is absent DiskBasis(coords, shape=(Nphi, Nr)) RealFourier / ComplexFourier(phi) × DiskBasis(r) same polynomial space for each \(m\) ; the pipe-flow eigenvalues equal Dedalus’s to round-off AnnulusBasis × AnnulusBasis(r) approximate

heading: The official Dedalus examples
text: Every official Dedalus 3 example was translated unmodified, which tests the coverage of the translator. Where the comparison is possible, both codes then ran the same script (smaller sizes, a short time, a deterministic initial condition instead of fill_random , a fixed dt instead of the CFL): KdV–Burgers, Rayleigh–Bénard, the 2D shear flow, the Poisson problem, the Rayleigh–Bénard eigenvalue problem and the pipe-flow eigenvalues agree to round-off. The spherical examples (sphere, shell, ball) use geometries that Conatus has, but their translation is not automatic yet: write them as native models ( Geometries ).

heading: Diagnostics and visualization
text: Eulerian, Lagrangian and mixing diagnostics computed from the fields of a run, on the CPU or the GPU. conatus.diagnostics computes the classical Eulerian, Lagrangian and mixing diagnostics of a flow from physical values on a declared grid , with the same code on NumPy and CuPy. It never touches a solver: every function reads arrays and returns new ones, so a run with diagnostics is identical to the bit to the same run without them. Anything that is not defined by the data alone is refused with the reason, never guessed.

heading: Global properties during a run
text: sim.properties(every=n, name=...) evaluates global quantities of a running simulation every n steps (the role of Dedalus’s GlobalFlowProperty ): a property is an unknown, a component, or a function of the simulation; the reductions are max , min , grid_average (mean of the grid values), volume_average and integral (quadrature). It never changes the run: import numpy as np import conatus as cn m = cn . problems . native . kuramoto_sivashinsky ( L = 22.0 ) sim = m . simulate ( N = 32 , scheme = "RK443" , dt = 0.01 ) . initial ( u = lambda x : 0.1 * np . cos ( 2 * np . pi * x / 22 )) p = sim . properties ( every = 10 , u = "u" , energy = lambda s : 0.5 * s . grid ( "u" ) ** 2 ) sim . run ( step

heading: Checking an installation
text: python -m conatus doctor says what your machine can run (compiled core, GPU) and, for anything missing, what to do. python -m conatus doctor # text; exit code 0 if nothing required is missing, else 1 python -m conatus doctor --json # the same, machine-readable import conatus as cn rep = cn . doctor () # DoctorReport: rep.ok, rep.explain(), rep.to_dict(); a table in Jupyter Each line gives one of three statuses (ok / missing / warning), the version or value found, what it is used for and, when something is missing, what to do . Each probe is short, runs in a subprocess with a timeout where needed, and turns any failure into a report line. The whole report takes about 2 s. Required: Python 3.1

heading: Adjoints and sensitivity

heading: Checkpoints off the GPU and sweeps longer than one job
text: With Revolve ( checkpoints=k ) the checkpoints can live elsewhere than in device memory, and a reverse sweep (or an optimal-perturbation iteration) can be cut by a time budget and resumed by the next job. A copy moves bits unchanged: every store, and every cut-and-resume, gives the same result bit for bit as the uninterrupted device run. import numpy as np import conatus as cn from conatus.adjoint import FlowMap , VJPSuspended m = cn . problems . native . kuramoto_sivashinsky ( L = 22.0 ) sim = m . simulate ( N = 32 , scheme = "RK443" , dt = 0.01 ) sim . initial ( u = lambda x : 0.1 * np . cos ( 2 * np . pi * x / 22.0 )) solver , t0 , X0 = sim . solver , sim . t , sim . solver . heading: Discrete and continuous adjoint modes
text: The discrete adjoint (adjoint of the discretised operator) and the continuous adjoint (discretisation of the adjoint equations, derived symbolically with their boundary conditions) are both available, and compared: from conatus.expert import Y , compare_adjoints , parallel_shear_flow flow = parallel_shear_flow ( 1 - Y ** 2 , kx = 1.0 , kz = 0.0 , Re = 2000.0 , walls = "no-slip" ) bcs = [( f , 0 , side ) for f in ( "u" , "v" , "w" ) for side in ( "left" , "right" )] cmp = compare_adjoints ( flow , bcs , 64 , target =- 0.05 + 0.3 j , infinite_tol = 1e-10 ) print ( cmp . explain ()) # discrete adjoint vs continuous adjoint

heading: Wavemaker and base-flow sensitivity
text: From a direct mode \(\hat q\) and its adjoint \(\hat q^\dagger\) , the structural sensitivity \(S(x) = \|\hat q^\dagger(x)\|\,\|\hat q(x)\|\) locates where a localized feedback changes the eigenvalue most (the wavemaker). The sensitivity to the base flow gives the eigenvalue drift for any modification of it. On the linear Ginzburg–Landau equation both have closed forms: from conatus.expert import ( Y , base_flow_sensitivity , ginzburg_landau_exact , linear_ginzburg_landau , structural_sensitivity ) NU , GAMMA , MU_C , MU_2 = 2 + 0.4 j , 1 - 1 j , 0.34 , - 0.01 exact = ginzburg_landau_exact ( nu = NU , gamma = GAMMA , mu_c = MU_C , mu2 = MU_2 , n = 0 ) def gl ( mu ): # dq/dt = -nu q' + gamma

heading: Continuation and bifurcations
text: Branches of solutions followed through folds by pseudo-arclength, with branch points, Hopf points, cycles and codimension-two curves located on the way. Pseudo-arclength continuation follows a curve of solutions \(G(x, p) = 0\) by stepping along its tangent and correcting with Newton on the bordered system, so that folds are passed rather than hit. Events (folds, branch points, Hopf points) are located on the curve by bisection on test functions.

heading: Data-driven analysis
text: Dynamic mode decomposition and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition of snapshots, in the inner product of the physics rather than that of the array. Snapshots are vectors of values on a grid. Every decomposition takes a DataInnerProduct , built from the quadrature weights of the grid and per-component weights, so that modes are orthogonal in the energy norm of the flow. heading: Spectral POD
text: The Welch segmentation ( nfft , noverlap , window ), the treatment of the mean and one- or two-sided spectra are all arguments. See also: tutorial 13. Where a global mode is born, and what the data say about it (Towne et al. 2018); dmd , spod , pod , DataInnerProduct .

heading: Eigenvalues and stability
text: Normal modes of a linear problem, each with its backward residual, with spurious modes removed only by a declared test. A linear model with an eigenvalue, or the linearization of a nonlinear model about a base state, is discretised into the generalized eigenvalue problem \[ (L + \sigma M)\,x = 0 \] for each wavenumber. All finite eigenvalues are computed (dense QZ) unless you ask for a few near a target (shift-invert Arnoldi). Infinite eigenvalues (rows of boundary conditions) are counted and removed; every finite mode reports its relative backward residual \(\|(L+\sigma M)x\| / ((\|L\| + |\sigma|\,\|M\|)\,\|x\|)\) .

heading: An eigenvalue problem written as on paper
text: The Orr–Sommerfeld equation for plane Poiseuille flow: the eigenvalue c is declared, the base flow U(y) is a given field, the conditions are named by boundary. import numpy as np import conatus as cn m = cn . Model ( cn . Box ( y = cn . walls ( - 1 , 1 )), name = "Orr-Sommerfeld" , Re = 1e4 , alpha = 1.0 ) m . scalar ( "v" ) m . given ( U = lambda y : 1 - y ** 2 ) m . eigenvalue ( "c" , growth = "imag" ) m . define ( "L2(f) = dy(dy(f)) - alpha**2*f" ) m . equations ( "L2(L2(v))/(1j*alpha*Re) - U*L2(v) + dy(dy(U))*v + c*L2(v) = 0" ) m . at ( "walls" , "v = 0" , "dy(v) = 0" )

heading: Left eigenvectors and sensitivity
text: left = m . eigenvalues ( N = 64 , left = True ) # right and left eigenvectors j = int ( left . values . imag . argmax ()) mode = P . least_stable ( Re = 1e4 , alpha = 1.0 ) print ( f "dc/dRe = { P . sensitivity ( mode , 'Re' ) : .3e } " ) # from the left and right eigenvectors With left=True the result also carries the left eigenvectors \(y\) , \(y^H(L + \sigma M) = 0\) . They give the derivative of an eigenvalue with respect to any parameter, \(\mathrm d\sigma/\mathrm dp = -\,y^H (\partial_p L + \sigma\,\partial_p M)\,x \,/\, (y^H M x)\) .

heading: What you choose, what Conatus refuses to choose
text: The resolution N , the second resolution of the drift test and its tolerance. The growth convention of the eigenvalue ( m.eigenvalue("c", growth="imag") ). Whether flagged modes are flagged ( spurious="tail" , the default, or "none" ). Dense or sparse solution ( method= , target= , n_modes= ): never switched for you. The wavenumber k= of a periodic direction (or m= , kz= , ell= of a curvilinear one). A singular pencil (a missing or extra boundary condition) is refused with a rank report.

heading: Validation
text: Read the residual of the mode you use and its drift between two resolutions. The spectral tail of the eigenvector is checked by verify (see Resolution ). See also: tutorial 1. A first eigenvalue problem: Orr–Sommerfeld (Orszag 1971); eigenvalues , EVPResult , ParametricEVP , critical .

heading: Floquet analysis
text: Stability of time-periodic flows by the Hill method: the Floquet exponents are eigenvalues of one large, structured problem. For a linear system with a periodic coefficient, \(\dot q + L(t)\,q = 0\) with period \(2\pi/\omega\) , solutions are \(q = e^{\mu t} p(t)\) with \(p\) periodic. Expanding \(p = \sum_n p_n e^{i n \omega t}\) turns the problem into the Hill eigenvalue problem \[ \big(L_0 + (\mu + i n\omega) M\big)\,p_n + \sum_{m \neq 0} L_m\, p_{n-m} = 0 , \] block-banded, with time discretised spectrally like space. The exponents \(\mu\) are defined modulo \(i\omega\) .

heading: A first example: Mathieu’s equation
text: import numpy as np from conatus.expert import HillBlocks , exponents_dense a , q = 1.5 , 0.5 # Mathieu x'' + (a - 2q cos 2t) x = 0, period pi L0 = np . array ([[ 0 , - 1 ], [ a , 0 ]], complex ) C = np . array ([[ 0 , 0 ], [ - q , 0 ]], complex ) # -2q cos 2t = -q (e^{2it} + e^{-2it}) H = HillBlocks ( diag = lambda mu , n : L0 + ( mu + 2 j * n ) * np . eye ( 2 ), couplings = { 1 : C , - 1 : C }, Nh = 24 , size = 2 , label = "Mathieu" , omega = 2.0 , mass = np . eye ( 2 )) mus = exponents_dense ( H , finite_cap = 1e3 ) # every Floquet exponent, modulo i omega print ( H . explain ()) HillBlocks takes the diagonal block, the couplings by harmonic and the number of harmonics Nh . exponents_dense

heading: A discretised time-periodic problem
text: For a time-periodic flow given as a discretised problem, hill_from_plan builds the Hill operator from the harmonics of the base flow, and checks that the operator is linear in it: the blocks \(L_m\) of the formula above are read from the plan, not written by hand. No resolution is chosen for you: the spatial resolution, the number of harmonics Nh and the number of base-flow harmonics kept are all arguments.

heading: Any model about a periodic base flow
text: In the native layer, m.linearize(about={u: lambda y, t: ...}, period=P).floquet(N, k=..., method="hill", Nh=..., targets=[...], tol=1e-12) gives the exponents of one wavenumber, from the same operator as the transient gain ( Non-modal analysis ). The expert form conatus.growth.floquet_exponents(build, base_harmonics, kx, kz, method=..., fields=...) takes a linear problem per wave; method="monodromy" compares with the eigenvalues of the time-stepped monodromy matrix. In a spherical shell, where the Hill operator would be very large, conatus.floquet.shell_floquet uses the one-period map of the time stepper and Arnoldi iteration instead: Spherical shells .

heading: Validation
text: An exponent is trusted when it is found again: refine the spatial resolution and the number of harmonics Nh until its digits stop moving, and check that its residual ( residual of a SecantRoot , residuals of a native floquet result) stays at round-off. Exponents are defined modulo \(i\omega\) : compare them after folding the imaginary part into one band. See also: HillBlocks , hill_from_plan , secant_root , and the mathematics in Floquet–Hill analysis of time-periodic flows .

heading: Dynamics
text: Everything Conatus does with a model once it is written: stability, growth, invariant solutions, their branches, their symmetries and their sensitivities. The model you simulate is the model you analyse. A native model ( cn.Model ) gives its eigenvalue problem with m.eigenvalues(...) or m.linearize(about=...) , its time stepper with m.simulate(...) (the flow map that every search for an invariant solution uses), and its compiled problem with m.compile(N).problem for the tools of conatus.expert . Every result carries the residual that validates it and an explain() that lists the choices made. Page Question it answers Eigenvalues and stability Is this state stable? Where does it become unstabl

heading: Invariant solutions
text: Equilibria, travelling waves and periodic orbits found by Newton–Krylov–hookstep on the flow map of your own time stepper. An invariant solution is a state that the flow maps to itself, up to a symmetry: an equilibrium \(v(u) = 0\) , a travelling wave \(u(x - ct)\) , a relative periodic orbit \(\tau_\ell\,\Phi_T(u) = u\) . Conatus solves these equations with a Newton–Krylov method and a trust-region (hookstep) step. The Jacobian is never formed: each Krylov vector costs one linearized evaluation or time integration, exact for the discrete scheme.

heading: The flow map
text: The searches use the time stepper of the model, here Kuramoto–Sivashinsky on a periodic domain of length 22: import numpy as np import conatus as cn from conatus.expert import ( NewtonKrylovHookstep , equilibrium_eigenvalues , find_equilibrium , find_travelling_wave ) L = 22.0 m = cn . Model ( cn . Box ( x = cn . periodic ( L )), name = "Kuramoto-Sivashinsky" ) m . scalar ( "u" ) m . equations ( "dt(u) + lap(u) + lap(lap(u)) = -u*dx(u)" ) sim = m . simulate ( N = 32 , scheme = "RK443" , dt = 0.01 ) # the flow map used by the searches newton = NewtonKrylovHookstep ( tol = 1e-12 ) # accuracy required; algorithm controls defaulted print ( newton . explain ()) # budget, GMRES, trust radii, marke

heading: Equilibria
text: q = 2 * np . pi / L sim . initial ( u = lambda x : np . sin ( q * x )) # odd seed: u(-x) = -u(x) E1 = find_equilibrium ( sim , sim . solver . X . copy (), newton ) # the Simulation itself print ( E1 . explain ()) print ( equilibrium_eigenvalues ( sim . solver , E1 , n_modes = 4 , dense_max = 500 , arnoldi_tol = 1e-12 )) An equilibrium of a translation-invariant system is not isolated (every translate is one), so find_equilibrium works in the subspace of odd states \(u(-x) = -u(x)\) , where translations are broken; the seed must lie in it, which is checked. equilibrium_eigenvalues returns the leading eigenvalues of the Jacobian in the full space, translation mode included.

heading: Travelling waves
text: sim . initial ( u = lambda x : np . cos ( q * x ) + np . sin ( 2 * q * x )) TW1 = find_travelling_wave ( sim . solver , sim . solver . X . copy (), 0.7 , newton ) print ( f "c = { TW1 . params [ 'c' ] : .5f } , residual { TW1 . residual : .1e } " ) The speed c is an unknown, fixed by a phase condition. The residual is \(\|v(U) + c\,\partial_x U\| / \|U\|\) , evaluated in the full space. A solution whose speed term \(|c|\,\|\partial_x U\|\) is below the Newton accuracy ( TW_SPEED_TOL times tol times the scale of the solve) is an equilibrium, not a travelling wave: it is returned as an Equilibrium (kind "equilibrium" , params["c"] kept, the measured value in the notes). A Newton run that lands

heading: Periodic and pre-periodic orbits
text: find_relative_periodic_orbit(solver, X0, T0, ell0, newton, steps=..., reflect=False) solves \(\tau_\ell\,\Phi_T(u) = u\) for \((u, T, \ell)\) with time and translation phase conditions; reflect=True gives pre-periodic orbits \(R\,\tau_\ell\,\Phi_T(u) = u\) . The number of time steps over one period is part of the problem. floquet_multipliers returns the multipliers of the orbit and identifies its marginal directions. Seeds come from near-recurrences of a long run; tutorial 5. Invariant solutions: Kuramoto–Sivashinsky, L = 22 carries one to the published Floquet exponents.

heading: Thresholds and edge states
text: The boundary between initial states that decay and those that become turbulent is located by bisection on an amplitude. Conatus returns the threshold as a bracket and never counts an undecided run on either side: from conatus.expert import ThresholdBisection def fate ( a ): """Declared verdict for amplitude a: x' = -x (x - 1)(x - 2), x(0) = a, t in [0, 40].""" x = a for _ in range ( 4000 ): x += 0.01 * ( - x * ( x - 1 ) * ( x - 2 )) return - 1 if x < 0.5 else ( + 1 if x > 1.5 else 0 ) tb = ThresholdBisection ( fate , rtol = 1e-4 ) lo , hi = tb . run ( 0.5 , 1.6 ) # the threshold as a bracket ]lo, hi] print ( tb . explain ()) The verdict function is yours (a time integration and declared thre

heading: Validation
text: A solution is accepted on its residual, reported with the iteration history ( explain() ). Its stability is a separate computation (eigenvalues or Floquet multipliers in the full space). A solution found in a symmetry subspace may be unstable outside it (see Symmetry subspaces ). See also: tutorial 5. Invariant solutions: Kuramoto–Sivashinsky, L = 22 (Cvitanović et al. 2010); NewtonKrylovHookstep , find_equilibrium , find_travelling_wave , find_relative_periodic_orbit , ThresholdBisection , EdgeTracker .

heading: Invariant manifolds and slices
text: The unstable manifold of an equilibrium as a polynomial parametrization, connections between solutions, and the reduction of a continuous symmetry by a slice. These tools treat the reduced coordinates of a solver (its active degrees of freedom, possibly in an invariant subspace) as a dynamical system. The examples below start from the equilibrium E1 and the travelling wave TW1 of Invariant solutions .

heading: Unstable manifold
text: The parametrization method writes the unstable manifold of an equilibrium \(x_0\) as \(P(s) = \sum_\alpha a_\alpha s^\alpha\) , with \(P(0) = x_0\) and \(DP(0)\) the unstable eigenvectors, and solves the homological equations order by order. It is exact for a polynomial vector field, whose degree is declared and checked. from conatus.expert import ecs_system , unstable_manifold ks = ecs_system ( sim . solver , odd = True , degree = 2 , dense_max = 400 ) # active coordinates x0 = ks . space . active ( E1 . X ) W = unstable_manifold ( ks , x0 , order = 6 , degree = 2 , eigvec_scale = 0.1 , unstable_tol = 1e-8 ) print ( W . explain ()) print ( f "defect on the circle |s| = 0.5: { W . max_defect

heading: Symmetry-reduced slices
text: A continuous translation symmetry makes relative solutions drift. The first-Fourier-mode slice fixes the phase of the first Fourier mode: travelling waves become equilibria and relative periodic orbits become periodic orbits. from conatus.expert import FirstFourierModeSlice , FourierOps , slice_equilibrium_check slc = FirstFourierModeSlice ( FourierOps ( sim . solver ), border_tol = 1e-6 ) check = slice_equilibrium_check ( slc , sim . solver , TW1 ) # a dict of evidence print ( check ) The slice border (where the first mode vanishes and its phase is undefined) is detected and reported, never regularized. find_rpo_in_slice searches periodic orbits of the reduced flow. See also: unstable_manif

heading: Non-modal analysis
text: Transient growth of a linear operator, measured in the kinetic-energy norm. A stable linear flow can amplify a perturbation by orders of magnitude before it decays, because its eigenvectors are not orthogonal. Non-modal analysis measures that amplification in a declared norm, here the kinetic energy \(E = \tfrac12\int |\boldsymbol u|^2\,\mathrm dy\) computed with its exact Gram matrix.

heading: The operator
text: from conatus.expert import Y , max_growth , parallel_shear_flow , state_space # Plane Poiseuille flow, streamwise-constant mode kx = 0, kz = 2, Re = 1000 flow = parallel_shear_flow ( 1 - Y ** 2 , kx = 0.0 , kz = 2.0 , Re = 1000.0 , walls = "no-slip" ) desc = flow . discretize ( 48 ) # 48 Chebyshev coefficients per variable ss = state_space ( desc , infinite_tol = 1e-10 ) # energy-orthonormal generator print ( ss . explain ()) parallel_shear_flow builds the linearized Navier–Stokes equations about \(U(y)\,\boldsymbol e_x\) in primitive variables for one pair of wavenumbers; the base flow is a symbolic expression in Y . state_space removes the infinite eigenvalues of this descriptor system and

heading: Optimal transient growth
text: \[ G(t) = \max_{q_0} \frac{E(t)}{E(0)} = \|e^{t\tilde A}\|_2^2 \] G , t_opt = max_growth ( ss , ( 1.0 , 200.0 ), xtol = 1e-6 , n_scan = 60 ) print ( f "G_max = { G : .2f } at t = { t_opt : .1f } " ) A scan of n_scan times is followed by a bounded Brent search whose tolerance xtol you give. For a time-periodic base flow, transient growth uses the propagator of the time stepper instead (next section).

heading: Any time-periodic base flow
text: Linearize the model about a base flow that depends on \(t\) and give its period. The gain over \([t_0, t_0 + T]\) and the Floquet exponents of one wavenumber then follow from the same operator: The base flow \(U(y, t)\) is split into time harmonics \(U = \sum_m U_m(y)\, e^{2\pi i m t/P}\) (a discrete Fourier transform over 64 instants per period); explain() lists the harmonics kept and the size of the largest one dropped, and a base that is not smooth in \(t\) is refused. optimal_gain integrates all unit initial states at once with the implicit–explicit scheme you name ( RK111 , RK222 , RK443 ), the base-flow terms explicit at the exact stage times and \(dt = T/n_\text{steps}\) exactly. The

heading: What you choose
text: The norm (through the weights of the system), the resolution, the time window and the tolerance of the growth search. The threshold below which an eigenvalue counts as infinite is an argument ( infinite_tol ), reported with the gap that separates the two families. See also: state_space , max_growth , the gallery case Non-modal stability of plane Poiseuille flow: transient growth and the continuous adjoint (Butler & Farrell 1992) and the mathematics in Non-modal analysis: transient growth .

heading: Onset of convection
text: The critical Rayleigh number of Rayleigh–Bénard convection between no-slip walls, and the shape of its mode, in a few calls: from the ready linearization, then from the equations of a normal mode written by hand. A layer of fluid heated from below is at rest while the Rayleigh number \(Ra\) is small. The rest state loses stability at \(Ra_c = 1707.762\) , for rolls of wavenumber \(k_c = 3.117\) (Reid & Harris 1958). Finding it means solving two problems at once: for each \(k\) , the \(Ra\) at which the growth rate of the least stable normal mode \(e^{ikx + st}\) crosses zero (the neutral curve), and the minimum of that curve over \(k\) .

heading: From the equations of a normal mode
