Box ( z = cn . walls ( - 0.5 , 0.5 )), name = "RB onset" , Ra = 1708.0 , Pr = 1.0 , k = 3.1 ) m . scalar ( "u" ), m . scalar ( "w" ), m . pressure ( "p" ), m . scalar ( "T" ) # amplitudes of exp(i k x + s t) m . eigenvalue ( "s" , growth = "real" ) m . define ( "L(f) = dz(dz(f)) - k**2*f" ) m . equations ( "s*u + 1j*k*p - Pr*L(u) = 0" , "s*w + dz(p) - Pr*L(w) - Ra*Pr*T = 0" , "1j*k*u + dz(w) = 0" , "s*T - w - L(T) = 0" ) m . at ( "walls" , u = 0 , w = 0 , T = 0 ) # no condition on t

heading: What you choose, what Conatus refuses to choose
text: The resolution, the drift resolution and its tolerance, the bracket of \(Ra\) , the interval of \(k\) and the precision xtol of the critical value. A bracket without a sign change of the growth is refused with the growth at both ends (checked on every call) and the sub-brackets where a scan finds one. The critical mode is checked against a full QZ at the critical point: if another admissible mode were less stable there, the result would be refused. See also: Eigenvalues and stability ; tutorial 0. Getting started: convection between two plates (the \(w\) – \(\theta\) form).

heading: Tangent, adjoint and optimal perturbations
text: FlowMap is the time-stepping map of a solver, X_0 ↦ X_N, with its exact discrete tangent ( jvp ) and adjoint ( vjp ): the same schemes, the same operators, the same linear factorizations, transposed. Nothing is approximated by a continuous adjoint, so the dot-product test holds to rounding and the Taylor remainder is of order 2. NLOP builds on it: nonlinear optimal perturbations (maximum energy growth at a horizon T for a given initial energy E0) and, in the limit E0 → 0, the linear optimal gain.

heading: In the native layer

page: Docs · Tangent, adjoint and optimal perturbations
heading: In the expert layer
text: FlowMap(solver, nsteps, t0=...) wraps an IVPSolver : fm.jvp(X0, V) is the tangent at X0 , fm.vjp(X0, W) the adjoint, and fm.pair(a, b) the pairing for which vjp is the adjoint of jvp . NLOP.from_solver(solver, T=..., E0=..., fields=(...), t0=...) is the nonlinear optimisation on the same map. Test an adjoint with the dot-product error normalised by |W| |JV|: the raw relative error of a stiff map on random vectors measures its conditioning, not the adjoint. In a Cartesian solver the energy fields are the scalar velocity components ( u , v , w ); on the shell it is the vector u . heading: Symmetry subspaces
text: Computing in an invariant subspace of a symmetry group: fewer unknowns and isolated solutions, at the price of hiding what breaks the symmetry. When the equations are equivariant under a group (reflections, shifts, rotations by \(2\pi/m\) ), the states with a given symmetry form an invariant subspace. Computing in it divides the size of the problem and, for continuous symmetries, removes the neutral directions that make solutions non-isolated. Conatus uses symmetry subspaces in three places: Invariant solutions. find_equilibrium works in the odd subspace \(u(-x) = -u(x)\) of a periodic problem, where translations are broken ( Invariant solutions ). Exact coherent states of 3D shear flows are

heading: What a subspace hides
text: An instability that breaks the symmetry does not exist inside the subspace. A solution found there is not declared stable until its spectrum in the full space has been computed: equilibrium_eigenvalues and floquet_multipliers work in the full space, and symmetry_breaking_check reports the growth rates outside the subspace. explain() on a symmetry subspace states what it hides. See also: SymmetrySubspace , Reflection , symmetry_breaking_check .

heading: Which terms are implicit
text: In an evolution problem you do not split the terms into a left and a right side. Conatus does it, term by term, with one rule: a term linear in the unknowns (constant coefficients, parameters, given fields) is treated implicitly; a nonlinear term or a source is explicit. A term changes side with its sign, and explain() prints where each one went: Term placement (IMEX split, automatic; override with implicit(...) / explicit(...)): [0] momentum implicit grad(p) (linear, constant coefficients) implicit dt(u) (linear, constant coefficients) implicit -Pr*lap(u) (linear, constant coefficients) implicit -T*Ra*Pr*ez (linear, constant coefficients; moved from the right side) explicit -dot(u, grad(u))

page: Docs · Errors and what they mean
heading: Errors and what they mean
text: Every error says what is wrong, where, why it is refused, and what to write instead. Conatus refuses rather than guesses. When a problem is ill-posed, a choice is missing or a solver does not converge, it raises an exception that says what is wrong, where (equation, term, variable, group), why it is refused and a suggested fix — which it never applies for you (see Principles ). The last line of every message links to the section of this page named after the exception class. All errors derive from ConatusError , and each also derives from the built-in exception its code raised before 0.1 ( ValueError , TypeError , KeyError , RuntimeError , NotImplementedError , ImportError , FileNotFoundError

page: Docs · Errors and what they mean
heading: Warnings
text: A warning never replaces a result: the result is returned. A warning is shown once per line of your script, and explain() does not repeat every one (it keeps the base residual of a linearization, the group in a result’s header and a growth rule “inferred from the name”), so read the warnings. A statement that the answer may not be the one the call meant is a conatus.errors.CorrectnessWarning (a UserWarning , shown by Python’s default filters wherever it is raised): Warning When BaseStateWarning m.linearize(about=...) about a base whose steady residual exceeds BASE_RESIDUAL_TOL (not declared with base_residual="accept" ); refused in v0.2 GroupWarning eigenvalues() without k= on a periodic mod

page: Docs · Errors and what they mean
heading: ResolutionWarning
text: Derives from UserWarning A returned result is under-resolved by a declared measure: the mode an eigenvalue result selects has its energy in the last coefficients, a Floquet-Hill mode in its outermost harmonics. Raised as a warning, never instead of the result: the same sentence is in the result and its ``explain()``. Not an error class (``warnings.warn``).

page: Docs · Errors and what they mean
heading: CorrectnessWarning
text: Derives from UserWarning The returned answer may not be the one the call meant: it is about another base state, another group of modes, or a choice the call did not declare. Shown under Python's default filters wherever it is raised (never a ``DeprecationWarning``, which Python hides outside ``__main__``); the result is still returned. ``explain()`` keeps part of it only (the base residual in ``lin.explain()``, the group in the result's header, the growth rule "inferred from the name"; Where the message says "refused in v0.2", the same call raises from v0.2.

page: Docs · Errors and what they mean
heading: BaseStateWarning
text: Derives from CorrectnessWarning A linearization about a base state that is not a steady solution: its steady residual exceeds ``BASE_RESIDUAL_TOL`` and ``base_residual='accept'`` was not given, so the modes are not the normal modes of a flow that exists (accepted in v0.1, refused in v0.2).

page: Docs · Errors and what they mean
heading: GroupWarning
text: Derives from CorrectnessWarning An eigenvalue call without a group (no ``k=`` on a periodic model, no ``m=``/``kz=``/ ``ell=`` on a curvilinear one) solved one group only (k = 0, or the first group): the modes of every other wavenumber are absent from the result (required in v0.2).

page: Docs · Errors and what they mean
heading: DefaultChoiceWarning
text: Derives from CorrectnessWarning A choice that decides the answer was left out and the v0.1 default or guess was used: the growth rule of an eigenvalue guessed from its name (``m.eigenvalue("c")`` ranks by Im c), the top condition of ``this case`` (no-slip). Declare it; required from v0.2.

heading: The expert layer
text: Under every native model there is an explicit problem that you can read, modify or write yourself: bases with their sizes, tau terms, the left and right sides of each equation. import conatus as cn m = cn . problems . native . rayleigh_benard ( Lx = 2.0 , Ra = 2500 , Pr = 1 ) # a native model comp = m . compile ( N = ( 64 , 32 )) # the native model at a resolution comp . problem # the expert problem (IVP, EVP, LBVP or NLBVP), as written by Conatus comp . fields [ "T" ] # its unknowns, taus included comp . ncc # data of the given (non-constant) fields print ( comp . explain ()) # every automatic decision plan = comp . discretize () # the discrete problem: groups, matrices, rank report sim = m

heading: When to use it
text: The native layer covers most problems. The expert layer is there for what it deliberately does not decide for you: conditions that couple several unknowns, or act on one component of a vector (free slip); symmetry subspaces, where the parity of each tau must be declared by hand; first-order formulations chosen by hand, or several equations sharing the taus of one unknown; bases outside the geometry catalogue (Legendre, Jacobi, mapped Chebyshev for infinite lines); options of the discretisation and of the time stepper (below). A name that exists in both layers means the same thing in both: cn.discretize(problem) is conatus.expert.discretize(problem) . conatus.expert.explain() lists what the i

heading: Resolution
text: The resolution is a tuple in the coordinate order, a dict by coordinate name, or an integer when the geometry has one coordinate: import conatus as cn m = cn . problems . native . rayleigh_benard ( Lx = 2.0 , Ra = 2500 , Pr = 1 ) # x periodic, z between walls m . simulate ( N = ( 64 , 32 ), scheme = "RK443" , dt = 1e-3 ) # x: 64, z: 32 m . simulate ( N = { "x" : 64 , "z" : 32 }, scheme = "RK443" , dt = 1e-3 ) A missing size, or an integer for a geometry with several coordinates, is refused. The default dealiasing factor follows the degree p of the products of unknowns: max(3/2, (p+1)/2) (3/2 for quadratic terms, 2 for cubic ones), and max(2, (p+1)/2) along Hermite/Laguerre axes, where no fac

heading: Limits
text: A Box has at most one bounded axis; two walled directions (a duct, a cavity) are refused with UnsupportedError . Free-slip and other conditions that act on single components of a vector unknown are written in the expert layer . Every geometry runs on the CPU and on a GPU ( backend="cuda" ); the fused nonlinear kernels are for Cartesian geometries ( GPU ).

heading: GPU
text: The same model runs on an NVIDIA GPU by adding backend="cuda" ; the arithmetic is double precision, as on the CPU. # requires: gpu import conatus as cn m = cn . problems . native . rayleigh_benard ( Lx = 2.0 , Ra = 2500 , Pr = 1 ) sim = m . simulate ( N = ( 256 , 128 ), scheme = "RK443" , dt = 1e-4 , backend = "cuda" ) sim . initial ( T = lambda x , z : - z + 1e-3 * ( 1 - 4 * z ** 2 )) sim . run ( until = 0.01 ) The backend is always your choice. Nothing falls back to the CPU on its own: a GPU request that cannot be served raises an error that says what is missing.

heading: Is there a GPU here?

heading: On a cluster
text: GPU work belongs in a batch job on a GPU node, never on a login node. Build the compiled core once for the architectures of your cards ( Installation , GPU section: tested CUDA and CuPy versions and the exact commands; A100 and L40S are the tested targets), then run your script in a job that requests one GPU. Recording the run ( The run registry ) keeps the host, the GPU and the job id with the results.

heading: Input and output
text: Two kinds of HDF5 files: analysis files , which hold what you asked to see (fields, derived quantities, numbers) at a fixed cadence, and checkpoints , which hold everything needed to continue a run exactly. Both are readable with h5py alone, and both carry the provenance record of the run (code version, environment, every numerical choice: Reproducibility and provenance ).

heading: A run split over two jobs
text: On a cluster a long run is a chain of jobs, and every job runs the same script. sim.resume_or_start(directory, u=...) continues from the latest checkpoint of directory when there is one, and starts from the given initial state otherwise (first job; the directory is created). An output without mode= then follows the same branch: its file is created on a fresh start (an existing file is refused there: mode="w" replaces it explicitly, e.g. after a first job killed before its first checkpoint) and continued after a restart ( mode="resume" : rows written after the checkpoint are dropped, the restarted run writes them again). sim.explain() says which branch was taken and which mode each file got:

heading: Analysis files
text: sim.output(path, tasks=..., every=k) writes every k steps, and the state at the start of the next run first ( initial=True , the default: a time series starts from the initial condition, as in Dedalus; a restarted job does not write that row again, and a start between two multiples of k writes none; initial=False starts at step k ; the output’s explain() says which). A task is the name of an unknown or of a component ( "u" , "u.z" ), an expression written as in the equations ( "dx(u)" , "0.5*u@u" ), or a function of the simulation in a dictionary ( {"KE": lambda s: ...} ) for anything else. In the file Content /scales/sim_time , /scales/iteration , /scales/write_number one entry per write /s

heading: Reading the files with other tools
text: The files describe themselves with plain HDF5 means, so other tools see named arrays on coordinates: every task has a dims attribute (for example ["t", "component", "x", "z"] ) and each of its dimensions is labelled and attached to its coordinate dataset as an HDF5 dimension scale ( t to /scales/sim_time , x to /scales/x , component to /scales/component ); vector tasks also carry component_names ; cn.io.read(path).to_xarray() gives an xarray.Dataset (dimensions t , component and the coordinates; iteration along t ; parameters and version as attributes). xarray is optional: without it the call says how to install it; for a 2D or 3D box or channel , sim.output also writes an XDMF sidecar <file

heading: Checkpoints and exact restarts
text: sim.save(path) writes a checkpoint now; sim.checkpoints(directory, every=k, keep=n) writes one every k steps and keeps the n most recent ( keep=2 by default: the latest and the one before it, in case a job is killed while writing). sim.restart(path) continues from a checkpoint and cn.io.latest(directory) finds the most recent complete one, in either format: checkpoint_<iteration>.h5 (written by sim.checkpoints ) and checkpoint_<iteration>.npz ( sim.save(directory / f"checkpoint_{sim.iteration:09d}.npz") ). The iteration is read from the file, a file still being written is ignored, two files of the same iteration in the two formats are refused (keep one format per chain), an empty directory g

heading: A run that starts at a time other than zero
text: sim.initial(u=..., t=t0) gives the state at the time t0 (default 0). Time-dependent forcing and boundary data are then evaluated from t0 , sim.t starts there, run(until=...) is read on that clock, every output row and checkpoint carries the times t0 + k dt , and explain() states the start time. Every checkpoint records the start time of its chain: resume_or_start(directory, u=..., t=t0) refuses to continue a chain that started at another time (the two scripts would not describe the same run), and a checkpoint written before this record is continued only without t= (native runs started at t = 0 until then). A non-finite or non-real t is refused. In a model with an unknown named t there is no

heading: What the map adds
text: The vertical coordinate is replaced by \(\xi \in [-1, 1]\) , \[ z = b(x) + \bigl(t(x) - b(x)\bigr)\,\frac{1 + \xi}{2} \] (Gal-Chen and Somerville, 1975), and every physical derivative is written by the chain rule, \[ \partial_z = J\,\partial_\xi, \qquad \partial_x\big|_z = \partial_x\big|_\xi + (A + B\,\xi)\,\partial_\xi, \qquad J = \frac{2}{t - b},\; A = -J\,\frac{b' + t'}{2},\; B = -J\,\frac{t' - b'}{2}, \] with the volume element \(\tfrac{t - b}{2}\,d\xi\,dx\) for integrals (the pressure gauge \(\int p\,dV = 0\) is over the physical domain). The metric is a polynomial of degree one in \(\xi\) : along the vertical the operators stay banded, exactly. Along \(x\) the functions \(J\) , \(A\)

heading: Conditions on a curved wall
text: A value ( T=... , u=0 ) is imposed on the surface itself. A derivative in a condition is the physical one along the coordinate: dz(T) at bottom is the vertical derivative, not the derivative along the normal. To impose a flux, write the normal as known fields of \(x\) : slope = lambda x : - eps * np . sin ( x ) # noqa: E731 b'(x) norm = lambda x : np . sqrt ( 1 + slope ( x ) ** 2 ) # noqa: E731 m = cn . Model ( box , name = "heat flux through a wavy wall" ) m . scalar ( "T" ) m . given ( "nx" , lambda x : slope ( x ) / norm ( x )) # outward unit normal of z = b(x) m . given ( "nz" , lambda x : - 1 / norm ( x )) m . equations ( "lap(T) = 0" ) m . at ( "bottom" , "nx*dx(T) + nz*dz(T) = 1" ) #

heading: Problems, schemes and limits
text: m.solve(N) (linear boundary-value problems), m.eigenvalues(N, ...) (one coupled spectrum for all modes) and m.simulate(N, scheme=..., dt=...) with SBDF1 – SBDF4 , RK111 , RK222 , RK443 . The implicit part is the coupled operator; nonlinear terms on the right are evaluated on the dealiased physical grid. Boundary data that depend on time are imposed at each stage time ( bc_time="stage" ; the default "auto" resolves to it and explain() says why; "rk" and "step" are refused). RK443 is then of order 2: the same errors as cn.Box with bc_time="stage" , and the same order as its default "rk" on this manufactured diffusion test. Cost: one sparse LU of the coupled system (all Fourier modes). Measured

heading: IR and operators
text: The expert layer writes problems with Python objects: fields, parameters and operators that build an exact symbolic expression. A Conatus script is written in a small symbolic language, the IR (intermediate representation): fields, parameters and operators build an immutable, hashed expression tree. Nothing is discretized until you call discretize . Everything below comes from a single import: from conatus.expert import * # IR, bases, problems, solvers, time stepping, dynamics toolkit conatus.expert re-exports the public objects of every user-facing module; name clashes are never resolved silently and are listed by conatus.expert.explain() (see explain() and the Methods paragraph ).

heading: Linearization and transposes
text: linearize(ivp, around={u: U, ...}, eigenvalue=sigma) (also ivp.linearize(...) ) differentiates every equation, boundary condition and gauge symbolically and replaces dt by sigma : the result is an EVP whose eigenvalue is the temporal growth rate. Base states are fields (NCCs); perturbation unknowns are named d<name> . The symmetry of the nonlinear problem is not inherited (a perturbation may break it): pass symmetry= explicitly ( 3. Symmetries and symmetry subspaces ). heading: Left eigenvectors and the physical adjoint
text: The adjoint of an operator depends on the inner product. InnerProduct(plan, weights={...}) is the weighted \(L^2\) product \(\sum_v w_v \int \bar v_1 v_2\,dV\) on the field unknowns of a group, with exact Gram matrices (closed-form \(\int T_m T_n\) for Chebyshev, exact Fourier norms); tau and constant unknowns get weight 0. Its adjoint(A) is \[ A^\dagger = W^{-1} A^{H} W , \] refused when \(W\) is singular, which is the case as soon as the group has tau columns: ValueError: Gram matrix is singular (tau or zero-weight unknowns): the adjoint for this inner product is not defined on the full column space. Use left eigenvectors (solve_dense(..., left=True)) for eigenvalue sensitivities, or a tau

heading: Ready problems and native models
text: Two functions share each name, one per layer: cn.problems.rayleigh_benard(Nx=, Nz=, ...) is the expert ready problem (a Ready , resolution in the call), cn.problems.native.rayleigh_benard(Lx=, Ra=, Pr=) the native model (a cn.Model , resolution at simulate ); start with the native one. A ready problem is an expert-layer object (its taus and bases are written out, so that it can be read and modified line by line; The expert layer ). Every one of them also exists as a native model, in cn.problems.native , written as on paper, with the same equations, units and reference as its expert counterpart: Native function Returns Same as the expert rayleigh_benard , channel , plane_couette , pipe , tayl

heading: Reproducibility and provenance
text: A number is only useful if you can say which code, which numerics and which machine produced it; Conatus records this when the computation runs, not afterwards. For runs you want to keep and query, use the run registry , which stores the same record with the results. This page describes the record itself.

heading: Provenance records
text: import conatus as cn from conatus.expert import provenance , provenance_record m = cn . problems . native . rayleigh_benard ( Lx = 2.0 , Ra = 2500 , Pr = 1 ) sim = m . simulate ( N = ( 16 , 24 ), scheme = "RK443" , dt = 5e-4 ) rec = provenance_record ( sim . solver , seed = 0 , tolerances = { "newton" : 1e-12 }, out = "run_dir" ) print ( sorted ( rec )) # ['code', 'environment', 'extra', 'numerics', 'recorded_utc', 'schema', 'seed', 'started_utc'] print ( provenance . problem_hash ( sim . solver . plan . problem )) # structural hash of the problem provenance_record is conatus.provenance.record . The bare name conatus.expert.record is refused ( AmbiguousNameError ): conatus.telemetry.record (

heading: Determinism
text: Restart : checkpoints hold the multistep history; a restarted run is bit-for-bit identical to an uninterrupted one, on CPU and GPU, and a checkpoint loaded with different numerics ( dt , scheme, start-up) is refused ( Simulations and time steppers ). Cross-backend : fast paths (compiled core, CUDA, fused kernels, graphs) are compared with the NumPy reference backend at round-off tolerance, not bit for bit.

heading: Tutorials
text: The outputs shown in the tutorials are those of the scripts, executed as shown and included verbatim; the first line of each output says when and on which commit it ran.

heading: Resolution
text: The resolution report says, for each unknown and each direction, whether the spectral coefficients have decayed, and how many modes a target accuracy would need. import numpy as np import conatus as cn m = cn . problems . native . rayleigh_benard ( Lx = 2.0 , Ra = 2500 , Pr = 1 ) sim = m . simulate ( N = ( 16 , 24 ), scheme = "RK443" , dt = 5e-4 ) sim . initial ( T = lambda x , z : - z + 1e-3 * np . cos ( np . pi * x ) * np . cos ( np . pi * z )) sim . run ( steps = 10 ) rep = sim . plan . resolution_report ( sim . solver , velocity = "u" ) # a simulation, an LBVP solution, or data print ( rep . explain ()) rep . ok # every (variable, direction) resolved rep . recommend ( target = 1e-10 ) #

heading: The run registry
text: cn.runs records the computations you may want to find, compare, cite or re-run later, with their numerics, code and machine. It needs no service: an SQLite index plus one directory per run (a JSON record, an HDF5 file for series and fields, solver checkpoints) under a root you declare. Tutorial: 11. Record, query, reproduce: the run registry .

heading: Where runs go
text: Set $CN_RUNS to the directory you choose (or pass root= ); without it, a scratch directory of the project is used. A default that resolves under your home directory is refused: runs belong on scratch storage. cn.runs.explain() prints the root and every declared constant.

heading: What Conatus checks before the first step
text: The usual way of writing the wall conditions of a shell in a spectral code (the one of the Dedalus shell examples) creates, at fine radial resolution and small viscosity, a growing mode that belongs to the discretisation and not to the flow: the run blows up after a while, whatever the time step. The native layer writes the conditions in a form that has no such mode, at every resolution, and you do not have to know which. Before the first step, Conatus looks for any growing artefact of this kind in the implicit operator and states the result (the spurious tau modes line above, also in sim.explain() ). heading: Tau terms by hand
text: In the expert layer you place the boundary terms yourself; a rank check refuses an ill-posed system before any factorisation. Conatus imposes boundary conditions with the generalised tau method : for each condition, one extra unknown (a tau variable , constant along the bounded coordinate) enters a bulk equation through a lift polynomial, and the system stays square and banded. The native layer writes these terms for you ( Boundary conditions ); this page is for problems you write by hand.

heading: The short way: add_bc

heading: The rank report refuses ill-posed systems
text: Two checks run before any factorisation: On the problem , pb.explain() counts, per bounded direction, the differential order of the bulk equations, the lifted taus, the boundary conditions and the tau variables. A mismatch is shown as Status: CHECK (it can be legitimate: pressure gauges, mixed-order systems). On the discrete system , each group’s structural rank is computed. A system that is not square or not of full rank is refused with a RankError before the solver is built, instead of a “singular matrix” deep inside a factorisation. Forgetting one boundary condition: RankError: system refused before factorization: Unknown coefficient DOFs 24 Tau DOFs 2 PDE equations 24 Boundary equations

heading: Simulations and time steppers

heading: Time-dependent boundary data
text: A boundary condition whose value depends on time ( \(u(\pm1, t) = g(t)\) ) is a row of the system without time derivative. When it is imposed changes the order of the schemes, so it is a declared choice, bc_time , printed by explain() with the equations it concerns: bc_time What a stage imposes Observed orders ( \(u_t = u_{yy}/2\) , both walls moving) "auto" (default) "rk" when \(g'(t)\) is exact, otherwise "stage" (the reason is printed) as below "rk" \(g_i = g(t_n) + dt\sum_j H_{ij}\, g'(t_n + c_j dt)\) : the implicit tableau applied to \(g'\) RK443 2.8, RK222 / RKSMR / RKGFY 2.00, RK111 1 "stage" \(g(t_n + c_i dt)\) at every stage RK443 2.0 (stage order of its implicit part), RK222 / RKSM

heading: Choosing the time step
text: Conatus never changes dt . Two indicators help you choose it, and they answer different questions: CFL ( sim.cfl("u", safety=0.5) ) is the advective stability limit of the current state, \(\Delta t_{\rm cfl} = \text{safety} / \max \sum_i |u_i|/\Delta x_i\) . It is a stability bound, not an error estimate. Temporal error : EmbeddedError(sim.solver) compares one step with a lower-order companion on the same data (SBDF \(q\) against SBDF \(q{-}1\) , RK443 against RK222, RKSMR or RKGFY against RK111; refused for the CN family, which has no companion) and reports the difference. It adapts dt only if you ask, with adapt=True and an explicit tol= . import numpy as np import conatus as cn m = cn . p

heading: A run that blows up stops
text: A diverging run (time step too large, an instability the resolution cannot follow) is stopped, never stepped on in NaN: the state is tested for NaN or inf every 100 steps, at the end of every run call and before every checkpoint or output write, and a cn.errors.NumericalError names the iteration, the time, the unknown and the last iteration checked finite, with fixes (smaller dt , sim.cfl , higher N ). One reduction over the state per check (one host synchronisation on the GPU, none inside a replayed CUDA graph): measured at about 0.1 % of the step cost on one CPU core (Kuramoto–Sivashinsky N = 64 and Rayleigh–Bénard up to 256×64). check_finite=10 checks more often, check_finite=False turns

heading: A run that is under-resolved or ill-posed is told
text: At each finite-state check the relative spectral tail of every unknown along every direction (the largest coefficient among the last 10 % of the mode numbers over the largest one, as in Resolution ) is measured on the coefficients in memory. Above RUN_TAIL_TOL = 1e-3 (about 3 % of the energy in the tail window; 1e-4 warned on the resolved flagship run, KS L = 22 , N = 32 , tutorial 5) a cn.errors.UnderResolvedWarning names the unknown, the direction, the tail and the time, once per run, and sim.explain() repeats it. Nothing is changed. Kuramoto–Sivashinsky on L = 22 with N = 8 (where max|u| reaches 64 instead of staying below 3) warns at t = 1 with a tail of 0.76; at N = 64 it does not. Cost

heading: Watching during a run
text: sim.run(steps=n, callback=f, every=10) calls f(sim) every 10 steps (the expert sim.solver.run(n, callback=f, every=10) calls f(sim.solver) ); the period is part of the run and has no default, and a number of steps or a period that is not an integer is refused, never rounded. sim.run(..., record=True) records the run in the registry and returns it ( The run registry ). A callback ends a run early by raising cn.StopRun ; with on_stop="return" the run returns and sim.stopped says why, with the default "raise" the exception leaves run : import numpy as np import conatus as cn sim = cn . problems . native . kuramoto_sivashinsky ( L = 22.0 ) . simulate ( N = 32 , scheme = "RK443" , dt = 0.01 ) sim

heading: Underneath
text: sim.solver is the expert time stepper ( IVPSolver ) and sim.plan the discretised problem. Options of the solver can be passed through simulate(...) : startup= , f_backend="fused" ( GPU ), complexify=True (cos/sin pairs solved as complex systems of half size). The expert layer describes them. In a spherical shell, border= chooses how the linear solve of each \((m, \ell)\) group is laid out ( "auto" by default, the same matrix solved exactly either way): see Spherical shells .

heading: What is computed
text: quantity(N=..., dt=...) is run five times: the three time steps at the finest resolution, and the three resolutions at the finest time step (the finest run is shared). Time : the observed order of convergence \(p\) from the three values; the Richardson value is shown beside the result, and the error estimate is \(1.25\,|q_R - q_3|\) , with the safety factor of Roache’s grid-convergence index (Roache 1994). With scheme_order , an observed order more than 0.3 away from it is flagged: the time steps are not yet in the asymptotic range. Space : spectral convergence is geometric; the ratio \(\rho\) of successive differences gives the estimate \(1.25\,|d_2|\,\rho/(1-\rho)\) . Differences that do n

heading: The mean of a statistically steady run
text: cn.time_average(series, dt=..., discard=k) gives the mean of a correlated time series after its first k samples (the transient is yours to judge: discard has no default), with its standard error from the integrated autocorrelation time. A batch-means estimate is printed beside it as a check, and a series shorter than about 50 correlation times is flagged. import numpy as np import conatus as cn rng = np . random . default_rng ( 0 ) # stands for the Nusselt number of a run, nusselt = np . empty ( 20000 ) # one value every 0.01: a correlated series nusselt [ 0 ] = 6.0 # with a transient for i in range ( 1 , nusselt . size ): nusselt [ i ] = 4.9 + 0.98 * ( nusselt [ i - 1 ] - 4.9 ) + 0.02 * rng

heading: Units and conventions
text: Unit systems make every change of nondimensionalisation an explicit, checked call. Published values are written in many nondimensionalisations: a plane channel alone has three Reynolds numbers (centreline, bulk, friction), and wavenumbers are scaled by the half-height or the full height depending on the paper. Silent factors of \(2\) or \(3/2\) are among the most common errors when comparing with the literature. The rule: the mechanics is generic, a study’s conventions are presets, and every conversion is an explicit call.

heading: Unit systems and convert
text: A UnitSystem(name, family, scales, reynolds) lists reference scales (length, time, velocity) with their definition and value in the family’s base units, and its Reynolds group. convert is the only way to move a number between systems: from conatus.expert import CHANNEL_SYSTEMS , convert half , full = CHANNEL_SYSTEMS [ "centreline" ], CHANNEL_SYSTEMS [ "bulk" ] print ( convert ( 1.020547 , "wavenumber" , half , full )) # 2.041094: alpha per h -> per 2h print ( convert ( 2.0 , "length" , half , full )) # 1.0: two half-heights = one height kind is one of length, time, velocity, wavenumber, rate, frequency, frequency squared, energy density, reynolds ; the factor is the product of scale ratios t

heading: Principles
text: No silent substitution. Basis, resolution, boundary treatment, dealiasing, time stepper, tolerances and inner product are written by you or printed by explain() ; Conatus suggests, it never modifies ( Principles ). Validation by residual. Every eigenvalue, steady state or orbit comes with its residual and a resolution check, never as a bare number. Every capability tied to a published value. Each method is tested against a published table or a closed form, and each tutorial ends on one.

heading: Who it is for
text: Researchers and students in fluid dynamics and applied mathematics who study stability, transition, pattern formation and invariant solutions, and who want to go from an equation to a validated number, then to a GPU simulation, with the same script. Unaquæque res, quantum in se est, in suo esse perseverare conatur : each thing, as far as it is in itself, strives to persevere in its being (Spinoza, Ethica III, 6). The origin of the name.

page: Docs · Lyapunov exponents, covariant vectors and ensembles
heading: What is computed
text: The Lyapunov spectrum is that of the discrete map \(\Phi_{dt}\) of the time stepper (an implicit– explicit Runge–Kutta scheme at fixed step), not of a separately discretised variational equation. Its tangent is exact: for one stage, \[ (M + dt\,H_{ii} L)\,\delta X_i = M\,\delta X_0 + dt \sum_{k} A_{ik}\, F'(X_k)\,\delta X_k - dt \sum_k H_{ik}\, L\,\delta X_k , \] with the stage states \(X_k\) of the trajectory and \(F'\) the symbolic Fréchet derivative of the nonlinear terms, evaluated on the same dealiased grid. The exponents of \(\Phi_{dt}\) converge to those of the flow as \(dt \to 0\) . Multistep schemes are refused: their tangent lives in an augmented state and carries the parasitic roo

page: Docs · Lyapunov exponents, covariant vectors and ensembles
heading: Algorithm
text: Benettin / QR : \(k\) orthonormal tangent vectors are advanced with the trajectory and re-orthonormalised by QR every few steps (positive diagonal of \(R\) ); \(\lambda_i = \frac1T \sum \log R_{ii}\) . Transients of the trajectory and of the tangent vectors are discarded before averaging, both with declared lengths. Statistical error : the average is split into blocks; the standard error of the block means is reported together with the lag-one correlation of consecutive blocks, which must be small. Covariant Lyapunov vectors (Ginelli et al. 2007): the \(R\) factors are stored, a backward iteration with upper-triangular matrices gives the coefficients of each covariant vector in the Gram–Schm

page: Docs · Lyapunov exponents, covariant vectors and ensembles
heading: Ensembles
text: An ensemble is \(B\) states of one discretised problem advanced together: per stage, one evaluation of the nonlinear terms for all members, one sparse product by \(M\) and \(L\) , one stacked banded solve. Parameters that enter the nonlinear terms become per-member coefficients; a parameter inside \(L\) gives per-member factorisations. The same machinery advances \(B\) trajectories times \(k\) tangent vectors at once, on the CPU or the GPU. The fate of each member (relaminarised, transitioned, in which basin) is decided by declared criteria, and transition probabilities come with a Wilson confidence interval.

heading: Pseudo-arclength continuation
text: A branch of solutions of \(G(x, p) = 0\) is followed in the combined unknown \(z = (x, p)\) with no privileged parameter (Keller 1977). From a converged point \(z_k\) with unit tangent \(t_k\) : predictor \(z_{\text{pred}} = z_k + \Delta s\, t_k\) ; corrector : Newton on the bordered system $$ (1) ¶ \[\begin{pmatrix} G_x & G_p \\ t_x^T W & t_p \end{pmatrix}\] (2) ¶ \[\begin{pmatrix} \delta x \\ \delta p \end{pmatrix}\] = - \begin{pmatrix} G \ t_k \cdot (z - z_{\text{pred}}) \end{pmatrix}; $$ next tangent : the same bordered matrix with right-hand side \((0, 1)\) , normalised and oriented like the previous one. At a fold \(G_x\) is singular but the bordered matrix is not, so the branch passes

heading: Events
text: Test functions are evaluated along the branch; a sign change between two points is located by a secant in arclength, each iterate being a corrected point: fold (limit point): \(t_p\) changes sign; branch point : the determinant of the bordered Jacobian changes sign; Hopf point : a complex pair of eigenvalues of the Jacobian crosses the imaginary axis (with the mass matrix: the generalised problem \(J v = \sigma M v\) ).

heading: Branch switching
text: At a branch point the new tangent is the null vector of the Jacobian that is not along the current branch; with a declared symmetry the pitchfork is classified and one half-branch is chosen. At a Hopf point a family of periodic orbits starts with a declared first amplitude. At a period-doubling point of an orbit the doubled orbit is started from the Floquet vector.

heading: Periodic orbits by collocation
text: Periodic orbits of low-dimensional systems (and of Galerkin truncations) are computed by orthogonal collocation on a mesh in time, with the period as unknown and an integral phase condition, as in AUTO and MatCont. Their Floquet multipliers detect limit points of cycles, branch points, period doubling and Neimark–Sacker bifurcations.

heading: Codimension two
text: Curves of folds and of Hopf points are continued in two parameters with minimally augmented systems (a bordered matrix whose last component vanishes on the curve). Along them, the cusp, Bogdanov–Takens, Bautin, fold–Hopf and Hopf–Hopf points are detected.

heading: Normal forms and amplitude equations
text: The derivatives of the right-hand side with respect to the state are exact: the second and third Fréchet derivatives \(B(u, v)\) and \(C(u, v, w)\) are derived symbolically from the equations. They give the cubic coefficient of a pitchfork and the first Lyapunov coefficient of a Hopf point (super- or subcritical), and the coefficients of the Landau and Ginzburg–Landau amplitude equations by a weakly nonlinear expansion.

heading: Curvilinear geometries: regular bases
text: Disks, annuli, pipes, spheres, balls and spherical shells are discretised with bases that are smooth at the axis and at the poles by construction. No condition is imposed at \(r = 0\) , and no term is ever regularised as \(1/(r + \varepsilon)\) .

heading: Disk, annulus and pipe
text: In polar coordinates \((\phi, r)\) each azimuthal mode \(e^{im\phi}\) separates. A smooth scalar on the disk of radius \(R\) has the form \[ f_m(r) = \rho^{|m|}\, w(\rho^2), \qquad \rho = r/R, \] with \(w\) a polynomial. A vector is written in spin components \(u_\pm = u_r \pm i u_\phi\) , which are smooth when \(u_\pm = \rho^{|m\pm1|} \times\) (polynomial in \(\rho^2\) ). In the ball the radial dependence of each \((\ell, m)\) is again a power of \(r\) times a Jacobi polynomial in \(2r^2 - 1\) , the three-dimensional analogue of the disk, so fields are regular at the centre. heading: Conventions
text: The resolution of a sphere direction is the number of degrees \(L_{\max} + 1\) . Coordinates are ordered \((\phi, r)\) on the disk and annulus, \((\phi, r, z)\) in the pipe, \((\phi, \theta)\) on the sphere and \((\phi, \theta, r)\) in the ball and shell; the native layer prints the bases it chose.

heading: Eigenproblems, residuals and the physical adjoint

page: Docs · Eigenproblems, residuals and the physical adjoint
heading: Convention
text: A linear eigenproblem is stored as a generalised pencil, one per group, \[ (L + \sigma M)\, x = 0 . \] Linearising an initial-value problem about a base state replaces \(\partial_t\) by \(\sigma\) , so \(\sigma\) is the temporal growth rate of the normal mode \(x\,e^{\sigma t}\) . A model may instead declare its own eigenvalue (for example the phase speed \(c\) of Orr–Sommerfeld), which may appear anywhere in the equations as long as they are affine in it.

page: Docs · Eigenproblems, residuals and the physical adjoint
heading: Solvers
text: Dense QZ on the full pencil. Because the boundary and tau rows have no \(M\) part, the pencil has infinite eigenvalues; they are detected from the homogeneous pair \((\alpha, \beta)\) and counted, never mixed with the finite ones. Left eigenvectors are available. Shift-invert Arnoldi for a few eigenvalues near a target, valid for singular, non-symmetric \(M\) . Before solving, the pencil is checked for regularity at a generic \(\sigma\) ; a singular pencil (a missing condition) is refused.

page: Docs · Eigenproblems, residuals and the physical adjoint
heading: Every eigenvalue comes with its residual
text: For each mode the relative backward residual \[ \eta = \frac{\lVert (L + \sigma M) x\rVert}{(\lVert L\rVert + |\sigma|\,\lVert M\rVert)\,\lVert x\rVert} \] is reported. A small \(\eta\) says the pair is an exact eigenpair of a nearby pencil; whether the eigenvalue is accurate also depends on its conditioning, which is large for non-normal operators such as shear flows at high Reynolds number.

page: Docs · Eigenproblems, residuals and the physical adjoint
heading: Spurious modes and the drift test
text: Tau discretisations of fourth-order problems can produce a few spurious eigenvalues of large modulus, sometimes with positive growth rate, that move by orders of magnitude when \(N\) changes. They are removed by the drift test: the spectrum is computed at two resolutions and only the eigenvalues found again within a tolerance are kept. The number of rejected modes is reported; nothing is filtered implicitly.

page: Docs · Eigenproblems, residuals and the physical adjoint
heading: Critical parameters and sensitivities
text: The sensitivity of a simple eigenvalue to a parameter \(p\) follows from the left eigenvector \(y\) : \[ \frac{d\sigma}{dp} = -\,\frac{y^H\,(\partial_p L + \sigma\,\partial_p M)\,x}{y^H M x}. \] Neutral curves and critical points are found by Newton on the growth rate with this exact derivative, safeguarded by a bracket. The matrices’ dependence on the parameters (including a wavenumber treated as continuous) is reconstructed exactly once, so a parameter sweep does not re-discretise. The selected mode is checked against a full QZ at the end: if another admissible mode is less stable there, the result is refused.

page: Docs · Eigenproblems, residuals and the physical adjoint
heading: Inner products and adjoints
text: The adjoint depends on the inner product. With a weighted product \(\langle a, b\rangle_W = a^H W b\) (for example the kinetic energy, with the exact Gram matrix of the Chebyshev polynomials), the physical adjoint of a matrix operator is \[ A^\dagger = W^{-1} A^H W, \] not the transpose. When \(W\) is singular (tau columns carry no energy), the adjoint is refused; left eigenvectors, which do not need \(W\) , are used for sensitivities instead.

page: Docs · Floquet–Hill analysis of time-periodic flows
heading: Floquet exponents
text: The stability of a base flow that is periodic in time, with period \(2\pi/\omega\) , is governed by a linear system with periodic coefficients. By Floquet’s theorem its solutions are \(x(t) = e^{\mu t}\,\hat x(t)\) with \(\hat x\) periodic; the Floquet exponents \(\mu\) are defined modulo \(i\omega\) (adding \(i k\omega\) only relabels the harmonics), and a real operator has \(\mu\) and \(\bar\mu\) as exponents. Conatus always reports the folded value and says how it folded it.

page: Docs · Floquet–Hill analysis of time-periodic flows
heading: Hill’s method
text: Instead of integrating over one period (a monodromy matrix), the periodic part is expanded in Fourier harmonics in time, \[ x(y, t) = e^{\mu t} \sum_{n=-N_h}^{N_h} x_n(y)\, e^{i n \omega t}, \] and the base flow \(U(y, t) = \sum_m U_m(y)\,e^{i m\omega t}\) couples harmonic \(n\) to \(n \pm m\) . Each harmonic is discretised in space with the same sparse spectral operators as a steady problem. The result is a block-banded matrix \(M(\mu)\) , block tridiagonal when the base flow has a single harmonic, and the exponents are the values where it is singular: either the roots of \(\det M(\mu)\) , found by a secant method from a declared seed, or the eigenvalues of the corresponding generalised pro

heading: Mathematics
text: Short notes on the methods behind Conatus: what is computed, in which form, and why. They are written for a reader who uses the library and wants to know what happens underneath; each one ends with the references it follows. The notes describe the discrete problem Conatus actually solves. Where the native layer makes a choice for you (a tau placement, a gauge, the implicit/explicit split), the note says which rule it applies; explain() prints the same decisions for your own model. heading: Invariant solutions: Newton–Krylov–hookstep
text: Equilibria, travelling waves, periodic orbits and relative periodic orbits are fixed points of a map built from the time stepper. Conatus finds them by a matrix-free Newton method with a trust region, and certifies each one by its residual.

heading: Formulations
text: Write the discrete flow map over a time \(T\) as \(\Phi_T\) (the exact map of the time stepper, with \(dt = T/n\) ), and the velocity field of the semi-discrete system as \(v(u) = M^{-1}(F(u) - L u)\) . Equilibrium : \(v(u) = 0\) . Travelling wave \(u(x - ct)\) : \(v(u) + c\,\partial_x u = 0\) , unknowns \((u, c)\) , with the phase condition \(\langle \partial_x u^*, \delta u\rangle = 0\) that removes the free translation. Periodic orbit : \(\Phi_T(u) = u\) , unknowns \((u, T)\) , phase condition \(\langle v(u^*), \delta u\rangle = 0\) against time shifts. Relative or pre-periodic orbit : \(S\,\tau_\ell\,\Phi_T(u) = u\) with a shift \(\tau_\ell\) and optionally a reflection \(S\) , unknowns

heading: Newton–Krylov
text: The Newton correction solves \(J\,\delta z = -R(z)\) by GMRES. The Jacobian is never formed: its products with a vector use the exact tangent of the time stepper ( Lyapunov exponents, covariant vectors and ensembles and the adjoint pages describe the same tangent), and the derivative with respect to \(T\) is the velocity at the end point.

heading: Hookstep
text: GMRES gives an Arnoldi basis \(V_{m+1}\) and a Hessenberg matrix \(\bar H\) . The Newton step minimises \(\lVert \beta e_1 - \bar H y\rVert\) . If it is longer than the trust radius \(\Delta\) , the hookstep (Viswanath 2007) replaces it by \[ y(\mu) = W\,\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\frac{s_i}{s_i^2 + \mu}\right) U^T \beta e_1, \qquad \lVert y(\mu)\rVert = \Delta, \] from the singular value decomposition \(\bar H = U\,\mathrm{diag}(s)\,W^T\) , with \(\mu\) found by bisection. The radius follows the ratio of actual to predicted reduction: halved and retried in the same Krylov space when the step is poor, doubled when it is good at the boundary. Every tolerance, budget and radius is an argument; a sea

heading: Stability of a solution
text: Once found, an equilibrium’s stability follows from the eigenvalues of its Jacobian, and a periodic orbit’s from its Floquet multipliers (eigenvalues of \(D\Phi_T\) , by Arnoldi on the tangent map). A solution computed in a symmetry subspace is declared stable only after the symmetry-breaking directions have been checked ( Symmetry subspaces, slices and phase-space geometry ).

heading: Edge states and minimal seeds
text: Between laminar and turbulent behaviour lies the edge of chaos. Bisection on the amplitude of an initial condition, repeated along the trajectory, tracks the edge state; the converged edge trajectory is then a seed for Newton. The same bisection on the energy of an optimised initial condition brackets the transition threshold of a minimal seed.

heading: Non-modal analysis: transient growth
text: Shear flows are governed by non-normal operators: perturbations can grow by orders of magnitude before decaying, although every eigenmode decays. This growth is measured in a declared norm.

heading: The norm
text: All quantities are measured in the kinetic energy of the perturbation, \[ E = \tfrac12 \sum_i w_i \int |s_i|^2\, dy , \] with declared weights \(w_i\) and the exact Gram matrix of the Chebyshev polynomials. With \(F\) a Cholesky factor, \(\lVert F x\rVert_2^2 = E(x)\) , and every operator norm below is a 2-norm after this change of variables.

heading: From the tau pencil to a generator
text: The discretised linearised Navier–Stokes equations form a pencil \(M x' + L x = 0\) with infinite eigenvalues (continuity, boundary rows, taus). An ordered generalised Schur decomposition separates the finite part, \[ (-L) Z = Q S, \quad M Z = Q T, \qquad x = Z_1 q, \quad T_{11} q' = S_{11} q , \] and a thin QR of \(F C Z_1\) (with \(C\) the map to the physical state) gives the generator \(\tilde A\) in coordinates orthonormal for the energy. Then \[ \lVert e^{tA}\rVert_E = \lVert e^{t\tilde A}\rVert_2 , \] without any truncated eigenvector expansion.

heading: Quantities
text: Transient growth \(G(t) = \max_{x_0} E(t)/E(0) = \lVert e^{t\tilde A}\rVert_2^2\) and its optimal initial condition (leading right singular vector). Numerical abscissa : the initial slope \(\max \lambda(\tilde A + \tilde A^H)/2\) .

heading: Time-periodic base flows
text: For a base flow periodic in time the propagator \(\Phi(t_0, T)\) is built by the same implicit–explicit schemes as the time stepper, applied to all unit initial states at once: the base-flow terms are explicit and evaluated at the exact stage times, the time step is \(T/n\) exactly, and the gain is the largest singular value of \(F\Phi F^{-1}\) restricted to admissible initial states (those satisfying continuity and the boundary conditions). Whether inadmissible inputs are allowed is an explicit choice.

page: Docs · Spectral discretisation and the tau method
heading: Boundary conditions: the generalised tau method
text: With \(N\) coefficients per unknown and an equation of order \(q\) , the equation leaves \(q\) degrees of freedom free. The tau method adds \(q\) unknown scalars \(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_q\) (functions of the other coordinates) to the equation, multiplied by fixed polynomials, the lifts , and imposes the \(q\) boundary conditions as extra rows. In the ultraspherical form the lift of \(\tau_k\) is the last modes of \(C^{(q)}\) , so the taus only perturb the highest modes of the equation and the system stays square and banded with a border. You do not write taus. For a native model the compiler applies one fixed rule: each boundary condition constrains one unknown \(f\) , and its tau goes into th

page: Docs · Spectral discretisation and the tau method
heading: Well-posedness before solving
text: Before any factorisation each group is checked: number of unknowns (coefficients, taus, constants) against number of equations (interior rows, boundary rows, gauges), structural rank by bipartite matching, and, for small blocks, numerical rank by singular values. A missing or redundant condition, a pure Neumann problem without a gauge, or a Helmholtz problem exactly on an eigenvalue is refused with the group concerned, instead of producing a meaningless solution.

page: Docs · Spectral discretisation and the tau method
heading: Nonlinear terms and dealiasing
text: Products are evaluated on a grid (pseudospectrally) and transformed back. A quadratic product of two series truncated at \(N\) modes has \(2N\) modes; evaluating it on \(3N/2\) points removes the aliased part exactly (the “3/2 rule”); a product of \(p\) fields needs \((p+1)N/2\) points. The native layer reads the highest polynomial degree \(p\) of its equations and uses \(\max(3/2, (p+1)/2)\) in every direction by default (3/2 for Navier–Stokes, 2 for the cubic term of Swift–Hohenberg), and prints the factor with its reason; dealias= changes it. Terms that are not polynomial in the unknowns ( exp(u) , 1/T , a pointwise function) are listed by explain() : no factor removes their aliasing. The

page: Docs · Spectral discretisation and the tau method
heading: Infinite and semi-infinite intervals
text: A bounded coordinate can be mapped to the real line or a half-line by a declared map \(y = m(\xi)\) , for example \(y = L\,\mathrm{artanh}\,\xi\) or the rational map \(y = y_0 + L(1+\xi)/(1-\xi)\) . The derivative \(d/dy = \mu(\xi)\,d/d\xi\) with \(\mu = 1/m'\) is banded when \(\mu\) is a polynomial, and otherwise \(\mu\) is expanded to round-off like any variable coefficient.

page: Docs · Symmetry subspaces, slices and phase-space geometry
heading: Computing in an invariant subspace
text: If the equations are equivariant under a reflection \(S\) (for example \(x \to -x\) with \(u\) odd and \(T\) even), the solutions with \(S u = u\) form an invariant subspace \(V_S\) . Conatus can compute entirely in \(V_S\) : the user declares the symmetry and the parity of each scalar field (the parities of vector components follow: the component normal to the mirror changes sign), and the library checks that the equations and the boundary conditions are equivariant, and refuses otherwise, naming the offending term; keeps only the independent coefficients: along a reflected Chebyshev direction the polynomials of the right parity, along a Fourier direction cosines or sines, and only the taus

page: Docs · Symmetry subspaces, slices and phase-space geometry
heading: What a subspace hides
text: A computation in \(V_S\) cannot see instabilities that break the symmetry. explain() always says so, and symmetry_breaking_check computes the leading eigenvalue (or Floquet multiplier) in each of the other isotypic components, reusing the same discretisation with the opposite parities. A symmetric solution is declared stable only after this check.

page: Docs · Symmetry subspaces, slices and phase-space geometry
heading: Slices
text: A continuous symmetry (translation along a periodic direction) is reduced by a slice. In the first-Fourier-mode slice, each state is shifted so that the phase of its first Fourier mode is zero; the shift is reconstructed by integrating the phase velocity. Relative periodic orbits become periodic orbits of the reduced flow. States where the first mode vanishes (the slice border) are detected and reported.

page: Docs · Symmetry subspaces, slices and phase-space geometry
heading: Trajectories, sections and manifolds
text: Poincaré sections : crossings of a hypersurface in a declared direction are located on the dense output of the time stepper (or exactly, by a partial step of the discrete map); successive crossings give the first-return map. Unstable manifolds of equilibria : by the parametrisation method, a polynomial expansion in the unstable directions, then globalised by time integration. Connections : heteroclinic orbits between invariant solutions by shooting with projection boundary conditions onto the stable and unstable subspaces.

heading: The split
text: After spatial discretisation an initial-value problem becomes, in each group, \[ M \frac{dX}{dt} + L X = F(X, t), \] where \(X\) holds the spectral coefficients and the taus, \(M\) and \(L\) are the sparse matrices of the linear terms (the boundary and gauge rows have no \(M\) part), and \(F\) collects the nonlinear and forcing terms, evaluated pseudospectrally. Stiff linear terms (viscosity, diffusion, pressure) are treated implicitly and \(F\) explicitly. In the native layer the split follows one rule: a term that is linear in the unknowns, with constant, parameter or given-field coefficients, goes to \(L\) ; a nonlinear term or a source goes to \(F\) ; each term moves across the equals si

heading: Schemes
text: Two families are available, with Dedalus’s names so that results can be compared: IMEX Runge–Kutta RK111 , RK222 , RK443 (Ascher, Ruuth and Spiteri 1997). A stage reads \[ (M + k H_{ii} L)\, X_i = M X_0 + k \sum_{j<i} A_{ij} F(X_j, t_j) - k \sum_{j<i} H_{ij} L X_j , \] with \((A, H)\) the explicit and implicit tableaux. In these tableaux all \(H_{ii}\) are equal, so one factorisation of \(M + k H_{ii} L\) per group serves every stage of the run. Semi-implicit BDF SBDF1 to SBDF4 (Wang and Ruuth 2008): multistep, one solve per step; the first steps are taken with a declared start-up procedure, printed by explain() . The time step is fixed and chosen by you. A CFL estimate ( sim.cfl("u", safety

heading: Factorisations
text: Each group’s matrix \(M + k H L\) is banded with a border (the tau columns and the boundary rows). It is factorised once by a banded LU with the border eliminated through a small Schur complement (capacitance) system; all groups are solved together in one batched call, on the CPU or on the GPU.

heading: Watching the taus
text: The tau variables absorb the residual of the truncated equations. Their size along a run is a cheap diagnostic of resolution: a growing tau means the top modes are not resolved. Conatus can monitor them ( TauWatch ) and warn above a declared threshold.

heading: Exact restart
text: The state of a run (coefficients, time, step count and, for multistep schemes, the history) is written in full, so that a restarted run continues bit for bit.

heading: Principles
text: Conatus is written for people who publish the numbers it computes, and its code enforces the rules that follow rather than recommending them.

heading: 1. No silent substitution
text: A numerical method is a list of choices: basis and resolution, boundary treatment (tau and lift positions), dealiasing factor, time stepper and step, tolerances, inner product, definition of the adjoint. Conatus never changes one of these for you. It may suggest ; it never modifies . Concretely: Dealiasing is declared. Unless you give dealias= , a native model uses the factor \((p+1)/2\) for the highest polynomial degree \(p\) of its equations in the unknowns, never below 3/2 (3/2 for quadratic terms, 2 for cubic ones), and says so in explain() and in the Methods paragraph; a value you give always wins; an expert basis requires the factor. There is no opaque dealias=True , and explain() warn

heading: 2. Validation by residual, never by a bare number
text: An eigenvalue, a steady state or a periodic orbit is not “correct” because it looks right. Each solver returns what is needed to judge it: Object What is reported Eigenpair backward residual \(|(L + \sigma M)x|\) , left residual, resolution drift against a finer plan, spectral tail of the eigenvector Sensitivity \(\partial\sigma/\partial p\) Taylor test of the exact derivative against a central difference Newton solution (NLBVP, equilibria, orbits) residual history (quadratic convergence visible), spectral tail Time integration observed order of convergence, manufactured solutions, exact decay rates of known modes Floquet exponent convergence in resolution and in number of harmonics, determi

heading: 3. Every capability is tied to a published value
text: Each method enters the library with a test against a published table or a closed form (Orszag 1971 for Orr–Sommerfeld, Reid & Harris (1958) for Rayleigh–Bénard onset, Cvitanović et al. A test that only compares two backends of Conatus can hide an error common to both: each compiler and problem class also checks a non-zero dynamical quantity against an exact value. The tutorials follow the same rule: each ends on an assert against its reference.

heading: 4. Everything explains itself
text: Models, simulations, plans, solvers and results have explain() . A simulation also writes the Methods paragraph of a paper ( sim.methods() ), built only from what the objects hold, with the BibTeX of the cited methods. See explain() and the Methods paragraph .

heading: 5. Provenance
text: A run records its commit (and whether the tree was dirty), environment, parameters, tolerances and inner product. See The run registry and Reproducibility and provenance .

page: Docs · 1. A first eigenvalue problem: Orr–Sommerfeld
heading: 1. A first eigenvalue problem: Orr–Sommerfeld
text: Goal. Compute the least stable mode of plane Poiseuille flow at \(Re = 10^4\) , \(\alpha = 1\) , and the critical Reynolds number, with a residual for every number. Expected. \(c = 0.23752649 + 0.00373967\,i\) and \(Re_c = 5772.22\) , \(\alpha_c = 1.02056\) (Orszag 1971, J. Fluid Mech. 50, 689). Time: under a minute on one CPU core. Script: t01_orr_sommerfeld.py .

page: Docs · 1. A first eigenvalue problem: Orr–Sommerfeld
heading: The equation
text: For a normal mode \(v(y)\,e^{i\alpha(x - ct)}\) of the wall-normal velocity, with \(U = 1 - y^2\) and \(\mathcal{L}_2 = D^2 - \alpha^2\) , \[ \frac{1}{i\alpha Re}\,\mathcal{L}_2^2 v - U\,\mathcal{L}_2 v + U'' v + c\,\mathcal{L}_2 v = 0, \qquad v = v' = 0 \ \text{at}\ y = \pm 1 . \] The eigenvalue \(c\) appears linearly; Conatus reads the mass matrix off its coefficient.

page: Docs · 1. A first eigenvalue problem: Orr–Sommerfeld
heading: Solve and reject spurious modes
text: res = m . eigenvalues ( N = 64 , drift = 96 , drift_tol = 1e-6 ) # keep modes found again at N = 96 i = int ( res . values . imag . argmax ()) # least stable surviving mode print ( res . explain ( key = "imag" )) print ( f "c = { res . values [ i ] : .10f } backward residual { res . residuals [ i ] : .1e } " ) The tau method produces spurious eigenvalues with huge \(|c|\) . Conatus never hides them behind a threshold: drift=96 (i.e. drift_plan= ) solves the same problem at a finer resolution and keeps only modes that reappear within drift_tol . res.explain() says how many modes were removed and why, and every kept mode carries its backward residual \(\|(L + cM)x\|\) and its drift.

page: Docs · 2. A first initial-value problem: Rayleigh–Bénard 2D, CPU then GPU
heading: 2. A first initial-value problem: Rayleigh–Bénard 2D, CPU then GPU
text: Goal. Write the Boussinesq equations once, time-step them on the CPU, check that a small perturbation grows at the rate predicted by the eigenvalue problem of the same equations, then run the same plan on a GPU. Expected. Growth rate \(\sigma = 5.5425059\) of the \(k = \pi\) roll at \(Ra = 2500\) , \(Pr = 1\) (EVP of the same equations; the streamfunction formulation gives the same value); onset is at \(Ra_c = 1707.762\) (Reid & Harris 1958). CPU and GPU agree to rounding ( \(\le 10^{-11}\) relative). Time: about 10 s of CPU (2a); about a minute on one GPU, mostly start-up (2b). Scripts: t02a_rayleigh_benard_cpu.py , t02b_rayleigh_benard_gpu.py

page: Docs · 2. A first initial-value problem: Rayleigh–Bénard 2D, CPU then GPU
heading: The equations
text:
In thermal-diffusion units, \(z \in [-1/2, 1/2]\) , rigid isothermal walls: \[ \partial_t \mathbf{u} - Pr\,
abla^2 \mathbf{u} + 
abla p - Pr\,Ra\,T\,\mathbf{e}_z = -\mathbf{u}\cdot
abla\mathbf{u},\qquad \partial_t T - 
abla^2 T = -\mathbf{u}\cdot
abla T,\qquad 
abla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0, \] with \(T = \pm 1/2\) and \(\mathbf{u} = 0\) on the walls. They are typed as written: terms may sit on either side; the linear ones become implicit, the nonlinear ones explicit, and explain() lists the split (override with implicit(...) / explicit(...) ).

heading: A run over several jobs
text: A cluster job has a time limit, so a long run is a chain of jobs, and each job runs the same script. sim.resume_or_start(directory, T=...) continues from the latest checkpoint of directory when there is one and starts from the initial state otherwise; checkpoints writes exact restart files; output writes the fields and numbers you ask for. Without mode= , the output file is created on a fresh start (an existing one is refused rather than replaced: give mode="w" to replace it) and continued after a restart (rows written after the checkpoint are dropped and written again by the restarted run). import tempfile from pathlib import Path work = Path ( tempfile . mkdtemp ( prefix = "rb_chain_" )) #

heading: The same run on a GPU
text: The model does not change. Only the backend is chosen, explicitly: backend="cuda" in m.simulate(...) moves the state, the batched banded solves and the transforms to the device; f_backend="fused" evaluates the nonlinear terms with fused kernels (the NumPy "evaluator" remains the oracle). sim.solver.run_graph(n) captures one step as a CUDA graph and replays it, which removes the launch latency. runs , early = {}, {} for label , kw in [( "cpu" , dict ( backend = "cpu" )), ( "gpu" , dict ( backend = "cuda" , f_backend = "fused" ))]: # both choices explicit s = m . simulate ( N = ( 128 , 64 ), scheme = "RK443" , dt = 2e-4 , ** kw ) s . initial ( T = T_init ) s . run ( steps = 20 ) # compare here

heading: 3. Symmetries and symmetry subspaces
text: Goal. Compute the Rayleigh–Bénard onset mode in the subspace of solutions symmetric about mid-depth, with half the unknowns, and see what the subspace hides. Expected. At \((Ra_c, k_c) = (1707.762, 3.1163)\) (Reid & Harris 1958; Chandrasekhar 1961) the leading growth rate is zero to the published digits; the subspace gives the same eigenvalue to rounding with half the unknowns. The complementary class decays. Time: a few seconds of CPU. Script: t03_symmetries.py · Tests behind it: tests/algebra/test_symmetry.py , tests/evp/test_rayleigh_benard.py , tests/ivp/test_nonlinear.py .

heading: The idea
text: A symmetry is declared, never guessed. You give a group (here the reflection \(z \to -z\) ) and the parity of each field; Conatus then checks that every equation is equivariant and refuses otherwise, naming the offending term; builds bases of the invariant subspace (even or odd Chebyshev polynomials, cosines or sines) and drops the boundary conditions that became mirror images of each other; solves only there, on CPU or GPU. For a vector field you declare only the “scalar” parity: under a reflection the component along the reflected direction changes sign, the others do not ( du=ODD means \(u_x\) odd, \(u_z\) even).

page: Docs · 4. Nonlinear boundary-value problems and continuation: Bratu
heading: 4. Nonlinear boundary-value problems and continuation: Bratu
text: Goal. Solve the Bratu problem \(u'' + \lambda e^u = 0\) by Newton, see quadratic convergence reported, then follow the solution branch by pseudo-arclength continuation through its fold. Expected. The closed form \(u = 2\ln(\cosh a / \cosh a x)\) , \(\lambda = 2a^2/\cosh^2 a\) (Bratu 1914; Gelfand 1963), with the fold at \(a \tanh a = 1\) : \(\lambda_c = 0.87845767978129\ldots\) on \([-1, 1]\) ( \(= 3.51383071912516/4\) , the classical value on \([0, 1]\) ). Time: a few seconds on one CPU core. Script: t04_bratu.py · Tests behind it: tests/nlbvp/test_nlbvp.py , tests/continuation/test_continuation.py::test_bratu_branch_through_the_fold .

page: Docs · 4. Nonlinear boundary-value problems and continuation: Bratu
heading: The problem
text: \[ u'' + \lambda\, e^{u} = 0 \quad \text{on } [-1, 1], \qquad u(\pm 1) = 0 . \] For \(\lambda < \lambda_c\) there are two solutions (lower and upper branch); they merge at the fold \(\lambda_c\) and none exists beyond. A Newton solver alone cannot pass the fold: the Jacobian is singular there. Pseudo-arclength continuation parametrises the branch by its arclength instead.

text: import numpy as np from scipy.optimize import brentq import conatus as cn from conatus.expert import ContinuationSettings , NewtonSolver , NLBVPContinuation , grid m = cn . Model ( cn . Box ( x = cn . walls ( - 1 , 1 )), name = "Bratu" , lam = 0.3 ) u = m . scalar ( "u" ) m . equations ( "bratu: dx(dx(u)) + lam*exp(u) = 0" ) # no dt(): a nonlinear boundary-value problem m . at ( "walls" , u = 0 ) print ( m . explain ()) # kind, tau placement, dealiasing: all declared pb = m . compile ( 64 , dealias = 1 ) # dealias declared: exp(u) is not alias-free anyway; # 64 modes resolve exp(u) to 1e-12 up the upper branch The model has no dt() , and the equation is nonlinear in u : m.explain() reports a

page: Docs · 4. Nonlinear boundary-value problems and continuation: Bratu
heading: Newton
text: newton = NewtonSolver ( pb . problem , tol = 1e-13 , damping = 1.0 , max_iterations = 20 , params = { "lam" : 0.3 }) sol = newton . solve ({ pb . fields [ "u" ]: lambda x : 0 * x }) # initial guess u = 0 print ( sol . explain ()) # residual per iteration, observed orders Tolerance, damping and iteration budget have no defaults: they are choices, and they are printed with the result. sol.explain() lists the residual of every iteration and the observed order of convergence \(q_k = \log(r_{k+1}/r_k)/\log(r_k/r_{k-1})\) — about 2 here, the signature of an exact Jacobian. Non-convergence raises NewtonNotConverged with the history; it never returns the last iterate silently.

heading: Continuation through the fold
text: settings = ContinuationSettings ( ds = 0.2 , ds_min = 1e-8 , ds_max = 0.6 , adapt = 1.5 , fast_iterations = 3 , tolerance = 1e-12 , max_newton = 15 , max_points = 6 , dp_fd = 1e-6 ) cont = NLBVPContinuation ( newton , "lam" , settings ) branch = cont . run ( sol . coeffs , 0.3 , + 1 , p_bounds = ( 0.3 , 1.0 )) print ( branch . explain ()) ( fold ,) = branch . folds () # located by bisection on the tangent print ( f "fold: lam_c = { fold . p : .14f } " ) ContinuationSettings has no defaults either (step size and its bounds, adaptation factor, corrector tolerance and budget, finite-difference step for \(\partial G/\partial\lambda\) ). The branch starts on the lower branch at \(\lambda = 0.3\)

heading: 5. Invariant solutions: Kuramoto–Sivashinsky, L = 22
text: Goal. Find the equilibria, a travelling wave and the shortest pre-periodic orbit of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation on the \(L = 22\) domain by Newton–Krylov–hookstep on the time-stepper’s flow map, with their stability. Expected. Equilibria \(E_1\) , \(E_2\) (energies \(0.2609\) , \(0.4382\) ; leading eigenvalues of \(E_1\) \(0.1308 \pm 0.3341i\) , \(0.0824 \pm 0.3402i\) ), travelling wave \(TW_1\) ( \(c = 0.73699\) , energy \(0.4649\) ): Cvitanović, Davidchack & Siminos (2010), SIAM J. Appl. Dyn. Syst. 9, 1–33, Tables 5.1–5.2 and §5. Pre-periodic orbit \(\overline{pp}_{10.25}\) : leading Floquet exponent \(\mu_1 = 0.033209\) , \(\theta_1 = 2.0079\) (Ding & Cvitanović 2016, SIAM J. Appl.

heading: The system
text: \[ u_t + u u_x + u_{xx} + u_{xxxx} = 0, \qquad x \in (0, 22) \ \text{periodic}. \] It is equivariant under translations \(\tau_\ell u(x) = u(x + \ell)\) and the reflection \(R u(x) = -u(-x)\) . Invariant solutions come in families: equilibria ( \(\Phi_t u = u\) ), travelling waves ( \(\Phi_t u = \tau_{-ct} u\) ), relative periodic orbits ( \(\tau_\ell \Phi_T u = u\) ) and pre-periodic orbits ( \(R\,\Phi_T u = u\) ).

page: Docs · 8. Polar geometry: a drum, a pipe, two rotating cylinders
heading: 8. Polar geometry: a drum, a pipe, two rotating cylinders
text: The same workflow runs on the disk, the annulus and the cylinder, on regular bases, with nothing divided by \(r\) . Goal. Solve three classical eigenvalue problems in polar and cylindrical geometry: the modes of a vibrating drum, written as a native model on cn.Disk ; the linear stability of Hagen–Poiseuille flow in a pipe; and the onset of Taylor vortices between rotating cylinders. The last two come from the library of ready problems ( cn.problems ). Expected. Drum: eigenvalues \(-j_{m,n}^2\) , the squared zeros of the Bessel functions (closed form). Pipe, \(R = 1000\) : rightmost eigenvalues of \((m, k) = (1, 1)\) and \((1, 0)\) to 10 decimals (Meseguer & Trefethen 2003, J. Comput. Phys.

page: Docs · 8. Polar geometry: a drum, a pipe, two rotating cylinders
heading: Regular bases, nothing divided by r
text: On the disk each component is expanded in a regular (Zernike-type) basis \(\rho^{|m|}\,P_n^{(a,|m|)}(2\rho^2 - 1)\) , vectors are stored in spin components \(u_\pm = u_r \mp i u_\varphi\) , and every operator is a sparse map between these bases (Vasil et al. 2016). There is no axis condition to impose and no \(1/(r + \varepsilon)\) : regularity at \(r = 0\) is built in. You name the geometry and its wall; explain() prints the bases it chose. import numpy as np from scipy.optimize import brentq from scipy.special import jn_zeros import conatus as cn from conatus.expert import eigenvalues

page: Docs · 11. Record, query, reproduce: the run registry
heading: 11. Record, query, reproduce: the run registry
text: Every run can be found again, compared, re-run to the bit, and reused only when you ask. Goal. Record a small parameter scan, certify the runs that pass a closed-form check, query them, compare two of them, reproduce one bit for bit, and see the cache reuse an identical computation only when cache=True is given. Expected. Heat equation \(u_t = \kappa u_{xx}\) with \(u(x,0) = \sin 3x\) : the measured decay rate equals \(9\kappa\) (closed form) to better than \(10^{-9}\) relative for every run; the query returns exactly the two certified runs; reproduce() is bit-identical; with the cache off an identical call is computed again, with cache=True it takes no step and returns the recorded end stat

heading: Going further
text: @cn.runs.track("name", cache=True) records every call of a function (arguments as parameters, return value as results) and reuses identical calls on request. In a Slurm job the record also carries the job id and the nodes. The run registry describes every query key, statuses and lineage.

heading: 14. Coming from Dedalus
text: Write a convection cell as a Conatus model, read the same cell from a Dedalus script, and check that the two agree. Goal. The onset of two-dimensional Boussinesq convection between a hot and a cold wall: write it as a native Conatus model: equations as on paper, conditions by wall name, no tau terms; give a Dedalus 3 script of the same cell to cn.from_dedalus and read its line-by-line report; run the translation and compare it with the native model as the wall-normal resolution grows; optionally, run the script with Dedalus itself and compare it with the translation. Expected. The report has no unsupported line. The native model and the translation are two tau formulations of the same equati

heading: Translate and read the report
text: SCRIPT = os . path . join ( os . path . dirname ( os . path . abspath ( __file__ )), "rb_cell_dedalus.py" ) tr = cn . from_dedalus ( SCRIPT ) # read with `ast`, never executed; Dedalus is not imported print ( tr . explain ()) counts = tr . counts () The script is parsed with ast and read statement by statement by a restricted interpreter. Nothing in it is executed, and Dedalus is not imported. In the output below, look for: e_z*tau_z(u_bot) : a product of two vectors, which Dedalus reads as a tensor product. The report says outer . trace(Gu) : it becomes div(u) plus the tau term, and div(outer(ez, ...)) becomes dz(...) . Both are exact identities, and both are listed. dealias=1.5 , written i

heading: Run the translation
text: solver = tr . ivp_solver ( startup = "lower_order" ) # the script's SBDF2, dt and initial th solver . run ( tr . steps ()) # 40 steps, no Python time loop print ( f "translation: t = { solver . t : .3f } after { tr . steps () } steps, " f "max|u| = { np . abs ( solver . grid ( 'u' )) . max () : .3e } " ) tr.ivp_solver takes the script’s scheme and dt , and replays its th['g'] = ... line on the Conatus grid. SBDF2 is a two-step scheme: startup="lower_order" is the start-up Dedalus uses (one first-order step), written here explicitly.

heading: 15. Covariant Lyapunov vectors of Kuramoto–Sivashinsky: tangencies and the physical modes
text: The Lyapunov exponents say how fast perturbations grow; the covariant Lyapunov vectors say in which directions, and the angles between them say whether the tangent space splits cleanly. In the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation on \(L = 22\) the first eight vectors keep touching each other while the rest stay apart: eight “physical” modes carry the dynamics. Goal. Compute the twelve leading exponents and covariant vectors of KS \(L = 22\) from a native model with sim.lyapunov , check their covariance, and count the entangled modes from the domination of the Oseledets splitting. Expected. Cvitanović, Davidchack & Siminos (2010, p. 12): \((0.048, 0, 0, -0.003, -0.189, -0.256, -0.290, -0.310, -1.963

heading: Exponents and covariant vectors
text: res = sim . lyapunov ( 12 , transient = 100.0 , align = 50.0 , T = 200.0 , reortho_every = 10 , inner = "euclidean" , n_blocks = 4 , seed = 1 , starts = starts , zero_mean = "u" , covariant = True , clv_window = 40.0 , clv_backward = 40.0 , clv_checkpoints = 8 ) print ( res . explain ()) Every length is a time of the problem: transient (trajectory only), align (the tangent vectors align with the Oseledets directions), T (averaging), clv_window and clv_backward (the covariant vectors are computed over a window that ends 40 time units before the end, the time the backward iteration needs to converge). Each must be a whole number of steps or of intervals reortho_every * dt ; nothing is rounded.

heading: 16. Lagrangian tracers and a numerical dye
text: Tracers show where the fluid goes; a dye shows how it mixes. Both are only as good as the velocity they are given and the way they are advanced, so both are declared: the velocity at a tracer is the spectral series itself, the time integration has a stated order that the tutorial measures, and the dye is one more unknown of the model whose mass is written to its file. Goal. Follow tracers in decaying Taylor–Green vortices and measure the order in time against a path integrated to \(10^{-13}\) ; then shear a dye blob in plane Couette flow with tracers on the walls, and read both files back with xarray.
